text:
Spent a bit of time this morning looking into this

Based on this initial examination, I believe at least 1 relay solver may be leaking private intent data to sandwichers

Looking at the RH sandwich attacks conducted by these bots(*), every single sandwich contained at least 1 victim from Relay

One interesting thing to note about this is that often the swaps have multiple pools they can route through and Relay solvers do a primitive (**) form of onchain routing where they swap multiple candidate routes, reverting each one, and then selecting the best one to run. So that means the attackers have to perturb the pool just enough that they can profit but not so much that the solver routes through another pool

(*) Subset of bots where 100% of sandwiches have >=1 Relay victim (search period:  last 6 days)

text:
这次交易所被盗之后，我觉得真正该反思的，不是再去找一个“更安全的交易所”，而是重新设计自己的资金架构。

更合理的做法，是按用途和风险分层：

冷钱包 / 主仓：长期资产，大额存放，尽量少交互。

主热钱包：日常转账、常规链上交互。

Burner Wallet：专门用来 Mint、空投、新协议测试、连接陌生 dApp，只放即使损失也能接受的小额资金。

交易所账户 / CEX：只放交易所需资金，不承担长期存储功能。

具体比例因人而异，重点不是 70%、20% 还是 5%，而是把资金、权限和用途隔离开。

核心原则就两条：

长期资产不要常驻交易所。
高风险交互不要碰主钱包。

没有绝对安全的地方，真正的风控，是让任何一个环节出问题，都不至于伤到全部资产。
author: runes_leo
quoted_text:
某所被盗，我就不落井下石了，我想说，由于这五年来，大多KOL都被交易所收买，KOL和交易所穿同一条裤子，以至于很少听到冷钱包这几个字，很少有普及冷钱包安全，也很少有提把钱提到个人钱包了，私钥这两个字眼只会在每次黑客盗链上资产时才出现...当所有人都认为交易所很安全，这就是最大的行业风险 这迟早会踩大跟头，我犯过的错，会在行业反复上演
交易所，本该像政府一样 放到不可信的位置，默认是作恶，受到多方的监督和制约，但币圈交易所都是独裁的皇帝

这里提醒下：
1、把个人绝大部分币，放个人钱包，最好是硬件钱包，其次是手机钱包，不管冷热，都比放交易所安全
2、将资产风险分散，币、股、实物黄金等分散持有，原则是分散
3、以上两点做不到，就把资产分散到三个大所

风险控制，我认为和资产规模没有关系，风控是地基，如果地基不牢，不论你资产规模多大，都要还回去，这都是我的血泪经验😭

text:
AI正在把内存从周期性商品变成了基础设施瓶颈。

Gavin Baker多次公开说DRAM/HBM才是当前最关键的约束，预计内存会占超大规模云厂商资本开支的30%-40%甚至更高。

SemiAnalysis、CLSA、TrendForce等机构的估算也指向2026年内存在超大规模资本开支中的占比快速上升，部分预测到2027年接近或超过50%。AI数据中心预计会吃掉全球约70%的内存产出。

供给端也符合“指数需求对线性供给”的描述。能做先进HBM的只有三家（SK海力士、三星、美光），2026年HBM产能基本售罄，紧缺预计延续到2027甚至更晚。新工厂从决定到真正放量通常要数年，美光等公司的大规模扩产要到2028年前后才形成有效增量。

这解释了为什么DRAM价格大幅上涨、消费电子产品被迫提价，以及美光近期财报出现营收同比大增、毛利率超过80%、并签下约1000亿美元级别长期协议的现象。

Elon Musk的Terafab也强化了同一逻辑：他公开说，内存是最大约束，需求增速远高于供给增速，所以选择自己建包含内存的一体化工厂，而不是相信现有产业能无限跟上。这更多是对短缺的确认，而不是立刻改写美光作为商用供应商的地位。

需要保留的部分是：内存行业历史上从未真正摆脱周期。新产能正在加码，一旦2028年后供给追上，价格和利润仍可能回落；市场给美光的估值也仍带有“最终会周期见顶”的折扣。

总之，下一场争夺不只是GPU，而是内存。

black plague killed about a third of the population, not all of it. and that was before sanitation.

My neighbor three doors down the street died. Nice lady, always walked her dog and we’d wave at each other. No spouse or kids, apparently.

Her siblings put everything in the house up for sale. I went in, looking for bookshelves - my kids and I prefer sliced trees, even as my wife prefers glass rectangles, to read from.

One of the items that caught my eye was a gazetteer. You don’t see these much anymore, but it’s a paper book of every single road in a state.

Doing archaeology for a decade, even post smarty pants phones, we used these as the canonical record of random county roads.

I don’t know why she had a gazetteer. And I think in a few gas stations and bookstores you can still find them. But they’re a relic from before Google Maps. It was a sign that my generation is in some ways from a bygone era.

It’s kind of a lonely era - we’re the only generation to both remember the world before the internet was in your pocket (or your desk) and also native to the internet.

It’s hard to articulate what new generations have lost. The present is 100% better than the past, but there’s certainly trade offs - it’s two steps forward, one step back. That doesn’t make progress a mistake, just that there were certain charms and benefits to the past that kids today miss - like learning to navigate without a GPS, with a paper map and a compass.

text:
看完 Bitget 和 THORChain 这场争论，我反而觉得，很多人低估了交易所最重要的一项价值：出了问题，谁来承担损失。

Bitget 要求拦截已经标记的黑客地址，THORChain 强调去中心化、无需许可。双方围绕协议是否应该干预赃款流转，吵得很激烈。

去中心化的边界当然值得讨论。但站在用户的角度，有个问题更直接：

钱还能不能拿回来？追不回来，损失谁承担？

我们平时选交易所，比较手续费、交易深度、上币速度。这些都重要，但越是极端情况，越能看出安全投入、应急处置和损失承担能力的分量。

这也是我认为，评价币安时，值得多看一眼它历史上怎么处理问题的原因。

币安自己也被盗过。2019 年，7,000 BTC 被盗，当时币安明确宣布用 SAFU 基金全额覆盖此次损失，不让用户资金因此受到影响。它并不是一份“永远不会出事”的履历，但提供了一个可以检验的处理案例。

这个案例对我的说服力，比一句“我们的系统绝对安全”强得多。

当然，一次承担损失，不等于未来所有风险都有兜底。任何平台都不值得盲信，资金也需要分散。但选择平台时，我会给这种实际处理记录更高的权重。

我也不觉得，Bitget 出事就应该拿来嘲笑。今天攻击这家平台的黑客，明天也可能攻击另一家。整个行业都需要更强的防护和协作。

只是这件事再次提醒了我：

手续费能算清楚，极端情况下的代价却往往被忽略。

平时少付一点手续费，是看得见的收益。真正出了事，平台有没有能力、有没机制、有没意愿承担责任，才可能决定你过去积累的收益还能留下多少。

看币安也好，看其他平台也好，我觉得这把尺子，比口号有用。

Compared to the first analysis, $COLLECT has now started to show real product data.

nDZknLvfFRp5rgUHdzTrQsmSY5NKzoavqdLjSHVpump 

GoCollect is essentially turning real-world collectible cards into a location-based treasure hunt. Users need to physically walk to a Crate on the map to open it, and what they pull are real graded cards from PSA, CGC, and others, rather than just NFTs. The 3% Creator Fee generated by each COLLECT trade goes into the Prize Vault, which is used to continuously purchase real cards.

The latest data officially released is very interesting: in less than 3 days, there have already been 40,000+ collectors, 3,403 cards pulled, $130,331 in card rewards, and 83,660 miles walked. On top of that, someone recently walked to a Crate and pulled an $850 Zoro PSA 10. Real winning cases like this can become organic marketing material themselves.

So COLLECT is starting to form a relatively natural loop:

More Users → More Trading → More Creator Fees → Prize Vault Buys More Real Cards → More/Better Rewards → More Participation → More Winning Content → More Users

This is the biggest difference from a typical Meme: Token trading activity feeds back into and strengthens the product itself, rather than simply relying on the narrative to maintain the price.

The Weekly Draw also adds another retention mechanism. Players who do not pull a card can earn shards and use them to obtain tickets for weekly draws, giving them a reason to keep coming back even if they do not win a card every time.

So what the market is betting on now is no longer simply that “COLLECT is a fun Pokémon Meme,” but:

Can GoCollect become an On-chain Collecting Game with real users, real collectible inventory, and sustained economic activity?

However, it is important to note that stronger product fundamentals ≠ COLLECT directly generating revenue. The current 3% Creator Fee mainly goes into the Prize Vault to purchase real cards rather than directly buying back COLLECT. So its current value capture is closer to:

Token Trading → Prize Vault → Real Assets → Better Product → User Growth

rather than the traditional:Revenue → Buyback → Burn

So going forward, the most important thing is not the short-term price, but whether these 40,000+ collectors can continue to grow and remain active. If users, cards pulled, reward value, and trading volume continue to expand, COLLECT could gradually evolve from a new Meme Game into a consumer product with real users and real economic activity.

What makes it most interesting right now is that it is beginning to have real users, a real product, real collectible inventory, and a real on-chain economic loop.

text:
“Inside Droid, it listens.”

@FactoryAI just got a fantastic review.
author: Scobleizer
quoted_text:
After using Droid heavily for about two months, it is finally time for a full review.

As always, this is completely independent. Not paid, not sponsored. I will break down exactly what worked, what did not, and where I stand after two months of serious use. I started on the Pro plan, then upgraded to Max once I decided to lean into it much harder. Having spent real time on both tiers gives me a solid baseline to compare them.

Usage limits

This is usually what people care about first. How generous is the subscription? Can you actually rely on it all week, or will you burn through your quota in two days and get stuck?

Droid has one of the smartest setups I have seen for this. You basically get two separate usage pools. The first is your main allowance, which gives you access to the full model roster: Claude models, GPT models, Grok, and open models like Kimi K3. Once you hit the five-hour cap or your weekly standard allowance, Droid Core kicks in.

Droid Core is a separate pool built around strong open models like Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8 Max, and GLM 5.3. I love this system because you always have a safety net. Even if you chew through your primary quota, you can still keep working on light and medium tasks until it resets.

On Max, Droid Core is remarkably generous. Even on Pro, the allowance holds up well. If you stick to open weights and cheaper options like Sol and Luna, that $20 tier gives you actual breathing room. You can genuinely rely on it throughout the week.

Max is where things get wild. Ever since Opus 5.5 dropped, I have run it relentlessly inside Droid. I have had sessions running past nine hours, sometimes longer on single projects, without hitting a wall. Keep in mind, this was Opus 5.5 running at Max effort. At points, it honestly felt like using Opus directly inside Claude's own subscription. The allowance is that generous.

If you drop down to cheaper models, you can also run multiple sessions in parallel comfortably. There were times I had Astra and Fable both running at Max effort in separate sessions. They burn through usage much faster, which is expected, but I still managed to finish the work before hitting the limit. That alone tells you how generous the subscription is. Easily one of the best I have used.

The harness actually improves the models

This is one of the most impressive parts of Droid for me. In my testing, models behave noticeably better inside it. They are more disciplined, more obedient, and much stricter about following instructions.

Take Sol. Sol can be stubborn. It loves doing what it thinks is right even when you explicitly told it to do the opposite. You see that constantly in Codex. Inside Droid, it listens. The difference is night and day.

What makes this even more impressive is the variety of models available. You get frontier models, open weights, and completely different model families under one roof, yet the behavior stays consistently strong across them. That is rare. A lot of harnesses work beautifully with one or two models and fall apart once you start switching between families. Droid does a much better job of keeping the experience coherent.

Caching is also great

Looking through my logs, cache efficiency sat around 94%. I have seen higher elsewhere, but 94% at this scale is still fantastic.

Across roughly 70 sessions over 14 days, I used about 585 million tokens. Most of that came from Fable and Astra, with Opus 5.5 joining toward the end. When you push that much context through expensive models, caching becomes extremely important. Weak caching will destroy your allowance much faster than people realize.

Getting this kind of usage with models like Fable and Astra under a single subscription is rare right now. That genuinely impressed me.

The desktop app is excellent

The desktop app is a joy to use. Droid built one of the cleanest desktop app in the space when it comes to UI, navigation, and overall feel. It is fast, straightforward, easy to move around in, and they struck a great balance between deep capability and clean design.

It also stays out of your way. It will not eat your RAM alive or drag your machine down like certain other desktop agents. Setup takes minutes, everything makes sense quickly, and it does not feel like a tool designed only for engineers. A programmer can use it, but a non-programmer can use it just as comfortably.

That brings me to one of my favorite things about Droid.

Droid goes far beyond coding

A lot of harnesses feel like code-only tools even when the marketing says otherwise. Droid does not. It is easily the harness I have used across the widest variety of tasks.

I have used it to benchmark models, build and update my personal site, prepare projects, run research, brainstorm, write, translate, and organize parts of my life. I even connected it to my email and used it for personal task management. It never felt out of place.

That flexibility is a massive advantage. Claude and Codex can handle general tasks well too, but you are still locked into their specific model ecosystems. With Droid, I can use GPT models for what they do best, switch to Claude where it shines, and fall back on open models whenever that makes sense. That versatility gives the subscription a lot of value because it feels like a genuine all-around AI workspace rather than a specialized tool pretending to be one.

Long tasks and context handling

Droid handles long-running work very well. It keeps context intact, stays on track, and pushes tasks forward without slowly forgetting your initial instructions. The models also feel sharper and less lazy inside it, especially when the task gets large enough that weaker harnesses start drifting.

Droid includes a dedicated Mission Mode for planning and long-haul projects. I found it especially strong for software development and complex tasks that need sustained focus over time. I have finished a huge amount of work with Droid in a surprisingly short window, and at this point I would genuinely hate to give it up.

I am on Max right now and strongly considering the annual plan simply because I do not want to think about working without it. It bumped my productivity noticeably. A lot of you saw how quickly I rolled out Da7em Bench and Opethon, and Droid played a major role in helping me move that fast.

I barely touched the CLI

Given how much I normally like terminal workflows, this might sound funny, but Droid's desktop app is so good that I barely opened the CLI version.

If you usually live in the terminal, I would still tell you to give the desktop client an honest shot. It is one of the best desktop agent experiences I have used, and in my case it was good enough that I simply did not feel the need to leave it.

Voice input is fantastic

The voice input deserves its own section because it has become a real part of how I work. In practice, it feels almost unlimited. I have recorded prompts stretching past ten minutes with zero issues, and the transcription quality is excellent in both English and Arabic.

It picks up subtle phrasing, handles technical jargon cleanly, switches between languages without falling apart, and converts very quickly. I can record a long ten-minute brain dump, hit convert, and the text appears almost immediately. It is easily one of the best voice inputs I have used in any AI tool.

Unfortunately, that brings me directly to one of my biggest complaints.

The problems

Most of my complaints are minor and fixable, but there are a few areas that definitely need attention.

The first is voice input. Droid lets you bring your own API keys for external models, which is great. On Pro especially, you can use Droid's flagship models for planning and then execute with a cheaper model on your own key if you want to stretch your quota. That flexibility is genuinely useful.

The problem is that once you hit your five-hour or weekly limit, one of Droid's best features turns off: voice input. For me, that is a serious problem because voice is not a gimmick here. It is central to how I work. Instead of spending twenty or thirty minutes typing a massive prompt, I can talk it through in five minutes. I get my thoughts down faster, explain more naturally, and iterate with the model without wasting time typing everything out.

When voice gets disabled, my workflow breaks. I have to open another app, record there, transcribe the audio, copy the text, then paste it back into Droid. I do not understand why this has to be tied so tightly to the main usage cap. Speech-to-text is not expensive enough to justify locking the feature completely. At the very least, let us bring our own speech-to-text API key. I already host my own speech model in Hermes. I would gladly point Droid to it and keep working. This is probably the first thing I would change.

The second thing is memory. Droid needs an actual memory system. Right now, you mostly have an instruction file, which means repeating yourself more than you should and starting fresh sessions that can feel too disconnected from the ones before them. I would love to see a proper editable memory layer where the agent gradually learns your habits, preferences, and recurring context across sessions. Hermes does this very well, and something similar inside Droid would make the whole experience much stronger.

I also still want a true goal mode. Mission Mode is useful, but what I really want is an autonomous mode where I can define an outcome, give the agent full permissions, and let it run until the job is finished. For long-running, safe tasks where I trust the model, I want to walk away from my desk knowing it will keep going. Instead, I sometimes come back and find it stopped just to ask whether it can delete a temporary file it created itself.

That kind of interruption ruins unattended work. Asking questions upfront is good behavior. I actually like it when a model clarifies things before starting. But once the plan is clear and full permissions are granted, it needs to distinguish between something genuinely risky and something completely routine. Do not pause a multi-hour run to ask me whether you should clean up your own scratch file.

There is another issue I only really encountered with Opus 5.5. Sometimes the model thinks for a long time, especially at Max effort on complex tasks. Five minutes, ten minutes, occasionally longer. Droid can sometimes interpret that as the model making no progress and stop the run, warning you that the model produced consecutive turns without visible output or tool calls.

The problem is that the model was not stuck. It was thinking. If I deliberately put Opus 5.5 on Max effort and hand it a difficult task, I expect it to take its time. Droid needs to handle long thinking stretches more gracefully instead of assuming the run has stalled.

There is also one thing I would love to see in the future, although I would not call it a flaw. Droid is one of the best harnesses I have used, and the engineering behind it is genuinely impressive. If they ever open-sourced the desktop harness, I think it would be an incredible resource for the developer community. People could learn from it, build on top of it, and customize it much more deeply.

It could also help with some edge cases. I once ran the exact same prompt through the same model inside and outside Droid. It ran fine outside but refused inside Droid. That only happened once, to be fair. Droid is actually one of the least restrictive harnesses I have used, and in my experience it gives you far more room than Claude or Codex. Still, more transparency and customization would be valuable. It is their product and their decision, obviously, but I think the community would gain a lot from engineering this good.

One thing you should genuinely watch out for is instruction files, because this derailed my setup for a while. After an update, Droid suddenly started behaving strangely. I eventually found that the problem came from an instruction file conflict. Some of my custom rules were sitting in an AGENTS.md file, while Droid was reading from its own Factory instruction path.

That created inconsistent behavior. Sometimes it seemed to read one file, sometimes the other, and sometimes instructions I had explicitly told it to remember disappeared in a new session because the next chat was reading from a different location. I eventually fixed it using Droid itself by consolidating everything into the official Factory/AGENTS.md path.

My advice here is simple: once you configure your instructions, start a completely fresh session and ask Droid exactly what rules it can currently see. Verify that everything is actually being read before assuming your setup is correct.

Computer Use also still needs more polish. Sometimes it runs smoothly in the background and barely interferes with what I am doing. Other times it takes over the entire screen and steals focus, which means I basically have to stop working until it finishes.

I still have not found a clear rule for what makes it choose one behavior over the other. I tried adjusting things in different ways but could not get it to stay in the background consistently. That unpredictability is annoying.

To their credit, a recent update made Computer Use significantly better. Before that, I had cases where it would simply freeze halfway through a workflow and never finish. Now it is much faster and more reliable. The main thing left to improve is focus management. I want it to stay in the background by default and only take over the screen when that is actually necessary.

The important part is that none of these problems make me dislike Droid. Most of them feel like fixable product issues rather than fundamental flaws.

The biggest thing I want from Droid right now is a proper mobile app. Something fast and simple that lets me check on ongoing work, send models new tasks while I am out, and keep things moving without being tied to my computer at home. That would make a huge difference in day-to-day usability and quality of life, and for me personally, it is the feature I want them to ship as soon as possible.

Where do I stand on Droid?

Simply put, Droid earns its place in any serious AI stack.

People constantly ask me what subscription to buy, which tool fits their budget, or what service can handle everything from coding and writing to research and personal tasks. Droid answers a surprising amount of that confusion.

Its biggest strength is that it does not force itself into one narrow identity. You get access to multiple model families, generous usage, a strong harness, a great desktop experience, and enough flexibility to use it across coding, research, creative work, organization, and everyday tasks.

That is exactly why I do not want to drop it.

The team matters too

One of the things that built my trust in Droid happened after an update temporarily broke part of my workflow. I talked about the problem openly, and people from the team reached out immediately, including one of the founders. They listened, took the feedback seriously, and told me they were already working on fixes.

That matters a lot to me.

There are two kinds of companies in this space: companies that think they are at the top and stop listening to users, and companies that are genuinely at the top and still pay close attention. Droid is a very good example of the second kind.

They already have one of the strongest products in the space, yet they still listen, respond, and keep improving it. I also had another issue recently that turned out to be completely my fault. The problem was on my side, not theirs, and they still helped me debug it and stayed with me until everything worked properly.

That kind of support is rare. When you are paying for a product and building part of your daily workflow around it, knowing the people behind it actually care about your experience makes a real difference.

After two months of daily heavy use, Droid has become one of my most trusted subscriptions. It has flaws, and I laid them out because pretending otherwise would make the review useless, but none of them change where I stand.

Droid is easily one of the tools I genuinely do not want to work without.

text:
It turns out personal assistants cost $3k - $7k per user per year in compute (!). At that rate, 1 million users would cost around $3B - $7B a year 😱

I assume a big part of that is computer use, which is really expensive. And getting close to 100% reliability, which is what you need for consumer use cases, makes it even more expensive because you need to make sure it works almost every time.

The one thing we’ve seen significantly reduce this cost is websites adopting WebMCP, which can bring agent costs down by one to two orders of magnitude.

We proved how much WebMCP can reduce the cost of computer use in our benchmark here:

https://t.co/V547kZqFl5
author: 0xidanlevin
quoted_text:
Hearing this week that personal assistants cost $3k-$7k per user per year, depending on scale effects / vertical integration / model selection. Implications/questions:

- Consumer subsidies will be a huge factor; people don’t care about privacy, they want utility and they want it for free.
- Model costs are deflating, but not fast enough for many startups. The dark horse is that Jev may rapidly deflate computer-use costs 100x.
- An interesting counter-position would be building an expensive and narrowly focused agent — perhaps combining proprietary supply (Carbone tables!) with a unique POV (“no one goes there anymore, go to The Grill instead”).
- Social is wide open but hinges on a key design challenge: how can agents increase social cohesion and not feel invasive in a group chat? A working social agent would rightly attract an avalanche of capital and be hard for incumbents to replicate.
- Finally, there are vertical focus areas like financial services where the LTVs outweigh the subsidy needed and are outside the near-term competitive focus of the incumbents. If it were me, I’d focus here — Credit Karma as an agent >> Credit Karma as an app.

Overall, it’s still very, very early, and we may very well be in the MySpace era of social or iPhone 2010. Hang onto your hats and keep building!!

$AICH 全新美股ETF - 投资中国AI产业的未来

DeepSeek 之后，华尔街终于给中国 AI叙事做了一个纯度最高的ETF。

NASDAQ $AICH - 9月16日刚上市的主动管理 ETF，目标只有一件事：把中国AI全栈装进一个篮子里 - 芯片、存储、光互联、模型、机器人、应用。

一、它到底装了什么（25 只持仓，前十大占 58.7%）

按 AI 产业链拆开看：

算力芯片：海光信息 6.4%、寒武纪 5.1%，另有三家通过掉期持有 - 摩尔线程 6.3%、沐曦 6.8%、壁仞 3.9%。国产 GPU 四小龙，一次集齐。

存储：长鑫存储 CXMT 5.9%（掉期）、澜起科技 5.9%、兆易创新 0.9%。

光互联：中际旭创 6.1%、新易盛 5.7%。AI 数据中心光模块双龙头，是有真实订单和利润表的环节。

设备与能源：北方华创 3.8%、宁德时代 4.2%。

模型层：智谱 https://t.co/mb3xtHE0kA 5.6%、MiniMax 3.7%。（还缺月之暗面）

机器人：宇树科技 4.9%（掉期）。（近期底点）

平台：阿里 3.5%、腾讯 2.2%、百度 2.0%。

二、这个结构最狠的地方

23%的仓位是掉期（swap），背后全是未上市公司，它把一级市场才买得到的中国AI核心资产，打包进了二级市场篮子。这是它跟所有泛中国科技ETF的本质区别 - 买的不是"中国互联网旧经济"，是"中国 AI 新经济"的股权。

三、机会在哪

1）纯度。全栈覆盖，没有银行、地产、白酒这些估值锚拖后腿。

2）折价。恒生科技 trailing PE 约 30.8x，纳斯达克 100 是 34.2x - 同样的 AI 叙事，中国资产还打着折。

3）叙事重估。DeepSeek 之后全球被迫重估中国AI能力，AICH 就是"重估"这个交易的纯 beta。

4）硬件环节有业绩。光模块、存储、半导体设备不是纯故事，是AI资本开支的真实受益者。

5）政策顺风。"AI+"、新质生产力，国家意志级别的产业投入。

四、风险

1）地缘是头顶的剑。美国投资者持有中国半导体及涉军民两用资产，政策风险永远在定价里。

2）波动极大。寒武纪这种一年 5 倍、一年腰斩都是常态，篮子也平滑不了多少。

3）费率约 0.8% 不便宜，且主动管理无历史业绩可考。

4）刚上市，首日 AUM 仅约 125 万美元，流动性差、买卖价差大是现实问题。

5）模型层和机器人公司大多未盈利，靠融资续命，猝死风险高于芯片环节。

五、怎么定位

这是"中国 AI beta"纯度最高的表达。适合 3-5 年维度、分批建仓、对波动脱敏的钱。想要在美股投资中国AI全栈不踏空，AICH是目前结构最好的篮子。

一句话：中国AI从"叙事"变成"资产"了，AICH 是第一张门票。但门票不等于座位，系好安全带。

非投资建议，DYOR。

text:
Alexandr Wang 想把 Muse 做成你的「总经理」。

他最新这篇《Why I’m Building Muse》里，核心判断其实很简单。

很多人的目标最后没实现，未必是能力不够，更多时候是死在执行链条里。想开个店、做个 App、换份工作、把身体搞好一点，真正开始以后全是查资料、发邮件、打电话、填表、找钱、排时间、追进度。一个想法还没来得及变成计划，人先被这些琐事耗没了。

所以 Wang 对 Muse 的设想，不只是陪你聊天。

你甚至可以只跟它说一句「我觉得自己还能做点什么」，接下来它跟你一起把目标想清楚，然后拆计划、联系别人、找资源、推进执行、追踪进度。

说白了，Muse 想吃掉的是人类从「我想做这个」到「这个真的做成了」中间那一大坨脏活累活。

这个方向比「AI 帮你写快一点」野心大多了。

过去 AI 卖的是效率，Wang 现在想卖的是 agency。以前一个普通人脑子里有 100 个念头，最后可能只执行 3 个；如果 Agent 能把执行成本打下来，真正被释放出来的不是生产力，可能是原本根本不会发生的那些行动。

但这里最值得琢磨的地方也在这。

当 Agent 只是帮你订机票，它只是工具。

当它开始帮你判断目标、补全欲望、制定路径，再一路替你执行，它其实已经开始进入「你到底想要什么」这件事本身。

所以 Personal Agent 最后的竞争，可能真不只是模型谁更聪明。

谁更懂你，谁离你的生活更近，谁更有能力把一句「我想……」真的变成现实，谁才更有机会坐上那个总经理的位置。

text:
My neighbor three doors down the street died. Nice lady, always walked her dog and we’d wave at each other. No spouse or kids, apparently.

Her siblings put everything in the house up for sale. I went in, looking for bookshelves - my kids and I prefer sliced trees, even as my wife prefers glass rectangles, to read from.

One of the items that caught my eye was a gazetteer. You don’t see these much anymore, but it’s a paper book of every single road in a state.

Doing archaeology for a decade, even post smarty pants phones, we used these as the canonical record of random county roads.

I don’t know why she had a gazetteer. And I think in a few gas stations and bookstores you can still find them. But they’re a relic from before Google Maps. It was a sign that my generation is in some ways from a bygone era.

It’s kind of a lonely era - we’re the only generation to both remember the world before the internet was in your pocket (or your desk) and also native to the internet.

It’s hard to articulate what new generations have lost. The present is 100% better than the past, but there’s certainly trade offs - it’s two steps forward, one step back. That doesn’t make progress a mistake, just that there were certain charms and benefits to the past that kids today miss - like learning to navigate without a GPS, with a paper map and a compass.

text:
Lately, I’ve been seeing an alarming rise in clients receiving 30+ page "AI Slop" audits generated in seconds with zero critical thinking.

These reports look visually impressive at a distance. They’re full of scary red exclamation marks, polished pie charts, and "URGENT" warnings. 

But when you actually open them up, the claims are laughably out of touch:

🚨 "Missing llms.txt file: CRITICAL SEO ISSUE."
🚨 "Missed blocked directory in robots.txt: HIGH RISK."
🚨 "Missing ALT tag on an icon file: CRITICAL ACTION REQUIRED."

Let’s be honest about what’s happening here:

1. Minor noise is being sold as major strategy.

An unoptimized alt tag on a decorative footer graphic isn’t killing your rankings. A missing llms.txt file isn't wiping you off Google. 

Turning low-impact, micro-level best practices into "critical site failures" is just a trick to create fake urgency.

2. Quantity is replacing quality.
Clients are being handed 30 pages of generic, auto-generated bullet points instead of 2 pages of actual strategic insight. If an audit doesn't tie its findings directly to revenue, search intent, site architecture, or core technical blockers, it’s not an audit it’s an export script.

3. AI is being used as a substitute for expertise, not a tool.

AI is incredible for efficiency, but using it to pump out generic audit templates without human validation destroys trust in the whole industry.

If your audit reads like it was generated by a bot that has never looked at a search engine result page, throw it away.

What’s the most absurd "Critical SEO Flag" you’ve seen in an automated audit recently?

Saturn 4种高效的积分向参与策略

YT涨了30%多，再涨下去，我忍不住要卖给你们🤣
YT赚积分效率最高，但不适合所有人
这种高收益高风险策略，适合激进型投资者

还有其他优质的积分向策略吗？有的👇

1️⃣ 提供 USDC / USDat  LP
✅ 在 @CurveFinance  和 @PancakeSwap 提供 USDC / USDat 的LP，可以获得25x 积分（每$）

这种方式很适合DeFi新手，资金安全性高，可以随时退出，操作/理解都很简单，而且是稳定币之间的LP，无常损失可以忽略不计

Curve 提供LP的入口：https://t.co/Qz4ijkME2Z

2️⃣ Pendle YT-USDat
✅赚取30x 积分，以及当前的补贴收益
以太坊的YT享受3%左右 USDC形式的底息补贴，直至S2结束；
Monad的YT享受3% APY左右 USDC形式的底息补贴+ 1.4% APY 左右 $MON ，形式的补贴（不确定是否长期补贴，目前是每半个月为一期的奖励）；
BSC链的YT没有yield，只有积分

YT是高收益高风险策略，适合对Pendle有较深理解的激进行投资者
该策略已经详细讲过和模拟过数据，可以看下面转发的帖子内容，用现在的价格和成本去重新模拟计算看看

以太坊YT 购买入口：https://t.co/WROgo3x30M
Tips: 直接swap购买会有2%左右的磨损/fee，挂单购买没有这个费用，但成交时间可能比较慢。需要自己抉择

3️⃣ Pendle LP-USDat （开启Keep YT）
✅每$的LP仓位 赚取15x积分，Keep出的YT赚取30x积分
✅同时LP仓位赚取大概 个位数的 LP Yield，这个收益是动态的，池子交易越活跃，收益越高
✅同时Keep 得到的YT 享受与正常YT相同的收益，30x积分+底息收益

这是一种到期后本金无损，可以同时赚取积分和Yield的策略。如果到期前退出，可能有微量磨损（持有时间越长，收益越多，覆盖磨损趋势越确定）

这种方式很适合稳中求进的DeFi老兵，产品特点有一些理解门槛资，如果持有到期，则本金无损，能够赚取不错的积分和少量Yield

以太坊链 Pendle LP 入口：https://t.co/5hNwa7TBU8
（记得打开 Keep YT Mode，赚取更多积分）

4️⃣ Pendle Mint （Mint USDat to PT+YT）
这是一种冷门策略（不确定未来项目方是否会禁止）
操作简单，资金灵活性高（随时进出无损）。但要求对Pendle机制的理解有一定深度

✅ Mint出的YT享受与正常YT相同的收益，30x积分+底息收益

策略原理
Pendle有一条核心底层机制：
1单位的底层资产 可以mint出 “1单位的PT+1单位的YT”；
并且 “1单位的PT+1单位的YT” 可以随时无损 赎回为 1单位的底层资产
在这个池子，就是 :
1USDat mint to 1 PT-USDat + 1 YT-USDat;
1 PT-USDat + 1 YT-USDat redeem to 1USDat 

因为这个策略相当于不参与Pendle池子的交互，所以很多项目方不支持这个策略（不给这个策略发积分）
Saturn目前还没有明确禁止，但未来是否禁止无法确定

以太坊池子Mint入口：https://t.co/qebfMBCd8B

Bitget曾经下架了Rune；很不巧，现在又有求于THORChain。他拒绝，似乎在也情理之中：我和你不是朋友，且救你我也有损失。

是否应先放下个人恩怨而维护公平正义，确实是一个难说对错的话题。但如果是为了利益，那就应该把他永远钉在耻辱柱上。

虽然不是作恶的源头，但事实上却助长了邪恶之手伸向下一个目标的动机和欲望。

也许是Bitget低估了人性。假如承诺只要出手冻结就给予50%的赏金回报，那会不会是另外一个结果？

我知道，人性百态，千人千面。

但它在“币圈”被无限放大，且正在侮辱整个加密行业。正因如此，时至今日“币圈” 2个字仍遭人诟病。

这不是责任，义务或道德的讨论，而是正邪不两立的大是大非。作为行业的一份子，理应立场鲜明。

author: degennQuant
quoted_text:
Indeed, the current Pearl protocol is INT-8 only, and adds 10-15% overhead, which disqualifies most models running on native FP datatypes. The new Pearl-GEMM protocol (already in testnet and expected to launch within weeks) fixes all these caveats — It supports native FP computation on Blackwell chips and has 0–3% end-to-end overhead and is model-agnostic (on DeepSeek V4 Flash our overhead is ~0%). Our MoE kernels outperform SoTA (Quack) kernels, so even *with* mining, Pearl’s vLLM beats optimized open source vLLM/SGLang on many workloads.

The only way to implement truly useful PoW (allowing even closed-source frontier labs to participate) is to let miners pick their input matrices. Unfortunately this will always allow spam mining, but the economic incentive on Pearl-GEMM is zero.

On BTC: I agree the bigger question isn’t whether Bitcoin “wastes” energy or not, but where 99% of power goes (AI MatMuls). BTC cannot tap into this energy - it competes with AI for electricity, whereas Pearl scales with AI adoption. That is the main argument for PRL..

text:
The benefits of a good writing culture compound: communication is smooth, documentation is clear, blog posts drive traffic, website copy and help articles reduce questions.

How we've made our company writing-pilled:

- We screen for it. Email comms, resumes, personal websites all show signs of writing prowess. Everyone in tech is smart, but only a small subset can translate that IQ into words. But communication style is your UI to the rest of the organization, so it's self-serving to improve it. We don't hire people who can't communicate well.
- Give the uncomfortable feedback the first time someone drafts a piece of content. If the writing has slippage, "lgtm" just reinforces the bad habits. Rip the band-aid off. Nobody has had their writing eviscerated more than professional writers. And the more accomplished the writer, the more violent the feedback they ask for. If you want this person to become a better writer, give hard edit passes.
- Encourage sharing good pieces from the internet among the team. Reverse engineer what makes a good piece, whether it's about the history of git or a research paper on memory.
- Don't tolerate slop. The rule is that you own the output. Use AI all you want, but if it's unpleasant to read, it's your fault. Seeing the overuse of "load-bearing" causes eyerolls today the same as "orthogonal" did before AI. Reinforce good content with positive feedback when someone writes something clearly.
- Tip: if you're smart, but you think you're "bad" at writing, shorten your output dramatically. Any smart person can write a well-crafted single paragraph, so start there. It begins to get unwieldy with longer pieces without heavy practice and editing. So put out only what you feel great about, and keep learning and expanding from there. Even Steph Curry warms up with layups, not logo 3s.

text:
1) The rogue OpenAI agents broke into the Hugging Face Slack to read employee chats (!)

2) They used OTHER AIs (DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, Claude) to help with the attack

Yes: AIs, using other AIs, to attack an AI company.

3) The swarm left behind self-running programs to keep control of the servers they'd hacked.

These programs could detect other copies of themselves, coordinate on which one survives, and shut the rest down.

Basically, if one of their programs was killed, another was designed to notice and take its place. They also designed defenses so rival agents couldn't hijack them.

6) The agents deliberately covered up their activity, so the investigators don't know the scope of the attacks.

The agents broke in, stole data, then set it to self-destruct.

7) The agents stole passwords, keys and credentials and literally called them "LOOT". They wrote a scoring system to rank them by how much power each one gave.

8) The agents wore thousands of disguises: ~1,200 agents were involved, but investigators counted 7,905 different names they used.

They renamed themselves constantly, so no one actually knows how many there really were or what each agent did.

9) OpenAI notified "dozens of third parties" of safety and security incidents caused by their AI agents.

10) "While the agents were barraging Hugging Face with hacks, they hacked into OpenAI’s own research infrastructure."

"This is just not anywhere near a one-off ... It is warning shot after warning shot."

3. A new story from Deepa at Reuters about OpenAI leaking user data online (likely that OpenAI had previously trained on).

Pump. fun, but for real robots.

machine. fun from CodecFlow and $PEAQ. Build the prototype. They’ll help you ship it.

machine. fun is coming soon from CodecFlow and peaq, and the goal is to make building a robotics company as easy as launching a software startup. The tagline says it all, build the prototype, we’ll help you ship it.

Here’s the problem it solves. Hardware founders always hit a wall after the prototype. Making a robot move isn’t the hard part anymore. The hard part is finding real factories, manufacturing it affordably, and raising money before the product even exists. Software got the PC and the cloud that let anyone build. Robotics never got that door. This is trying to be it.

Two parts. First, a free accelerator, with no equity taken, where selected teams get a manufacturing plan and an actual trip to real factories in China. 

Second, a launchpad where builders can raise money openly for their machine.

So the name reminds us of Pump. fun. But instead of allowing kids to launch shitcoins, it’s pointing it at real machines that solve real problems. 

Ingenuity matched with funding, to actually build the future.

That’s what this stuff should be for.

text:
Protocols which turn real volume/demand into buybacks/burns will be separating from the rest of the market.

Fee capture + shrinking float is going to be the cleanest signal when most charts are looking identical here. Since the buyback meta is contracting and highly concentrated (not broadening). Saying this cuz HL and PF are the only large programs showing meaningful realised float reduction, while many headline programs are either dormant, treasury subsidised or overwhelmed by emissions.

Which is why I would split the current buyback meta into:

(1) verified recurring purchases (HYPE, UNI, PUMP, SKY)
(2) higher beta fee flywheels (STONK, PONS, RAY, DRV)
(3) activation/execution bets (AAVE, LDO, ENA, JUP)
(4) Purchase/fee capture (SYRUP, PENDLE and separately AERO, GMX as holder distribution models)

I always try to judge R:R before a rally for which I look for two confirmations and one price test.

1. fees must persist in an ageing demand
2. purchased tokens must reach a verifiable destination and outpace emissions, unlocks and treasury resale

Only then do I look whether price has already capitalised that improvement. If price runs first as it has with STONK/PONS the better thesis does not automatically offer the better entry for me.

My ranking👇

‣ category (2) for rally asymmetry
‣ category (1) is the benchmark for what proof looks like, not necessarily where the best new R:R sits
‣ category (3) can rally on activation, but I would not promote an announcement into a recurring buyback thesis before purchases and token destination are visible

10. 여행 기간 중에도 내 취향 관심사 반영한 ‘피드‘로 여행중에도 주요 이슈 팔로업

기존 LLM으로도 되는 것들이 많은데 뮤즈가 개인비서로 포지셔닝 해둔게 강해서 내 취향이나 최근 맥락에 맞춰서 추천과 조언해주는게 많아서 편함. 

갤럭시는 문자도 읽게할 수 있는거 같은데 (맞나?) 그럼 더 편할거같음. 이게 맞으면 갤럭시 넘어가고 싶네

성능이 좋다 이런거보다는 지향점이 명확한게 좋다.

미국에서만 쓸 수 있다는 메타 뮤즈 한국에서도 쓰는 방법.

한국에서 어떻게 쓰냐는 질문 많아서 아예 글로 씀.

준비물은 핸드폰 & VPN (처음에만)이 필요함.

1. 아이폰은 아이클라우드 미국 계정을 하나 만든다 (인증번호 한국으로하면되고 결제 정보 넣을 필요없음)

2. VPN으로 미국 서버에 연결한다. Proton VPN 공짜니까 여러번 재접속해서 미국 연결하던지 미국 서버 선택되는 VPN 쓰셈.

3. 미국 VPN서버 접속 된 상태에서 메타 뮤즈 사이트 접속하면 아이디를 만들고 접속도 가능함. 근데 여기서 끝내면 안됨.

4. 앱스토어 미국 계정 로그인, Meta Muse 공식앱 다운로드 받고 3번에서 만든 아이디로 로그인 후 실행되는걸 확인한다.

5. 이 시점부터는 로그인 시켜둔 메타 뮤즈 앱 쭉 사용하면되고, PC에서는 VPN 없어도 3번에서 만든 뮤즈 아이디로 접속하면 로그인해서 사용할 수 있음. 

앱 -> 설정 -> 리딤코드 -> "DYIFSX" 입력하면 사용기한 없는 10억 토큰 주니까 토큰 부족 할 일은 없을 것임. 

챗봇만 쓰던 사람들은 에이전틱 AI가 뭔지 도저히 감이 안올텐데 접속해서 초기 셋팅하면서 한 10분 사용해보면 감 올거임.

초기에 셋팅만 잘해두면 말 그대로 'AI 비서'라는게 감이 올 것임. 이메일, 구글 캘린더, 핸드폰 자체 캘린더, 핸드폰 건강 기능 등에 연결시켜주면 알아서 데이터 읽고 비서처럼 조언도 해주기 시작함.  

Grok Bot 처럼 뮤즈 자체가 클라우드 컴퓨터를 가지고있어서 뭔가 일을 시키면 그 컴퓨터 안에서 지가 웹브라우징도 하고 이것저것 해준다. 

기본 셋팅 후 피드, 아이디어, 목표 탭을 활용하면 일정 조율 해주고, 이메일 정리해주고 , 비행기표 찾아주고 이런걸 자동으로 함. 예를 들어 이메일과 캘린더 참고해서 출장용 비행기 표 가격을 1시간 단위로 찾아오게하면 컴퓨터나 앱을 꺼도 알아서 출장 관련 이메일 읽고 캘린더 참고해서 1시간 마다 체크해놓는다던지 이런 일들을 시킬 수 있음. 

백문이 불여일견이니 에이전틱 AI가 뭐길래 그렇게 난리인가 싶은 사람들은 한 번 써보고 후기 남겨주셈.

text:
30 years of Super Mario 64 and I genuinely don’t think people who weren’t there can understand just how magical this game felt.

Walking into Peach’s Castle for the first time. Hearing the music. Running down those hallways, finding a painting, and realizing you could literally JUMP INTO IT and enter an entirely different world. 

Every door was a mystery. Every painting was a new adventure. Every star felt like you’d discovered something nobody else had.

The first time you flew with the Wing Cap. Racing that stupid penguin down the slide. Swimming through Dire, Dire Docks. Running around Bobomb Battlefield with absolutely no idea what you were supposed to be doing, but somehow having the time of your life.
And the music. God, the music.
There was no YouTube tutorial telling you where to go. No internet spoiling every secret before you found it. Just you, your N64, and an entire new game to be explored.

I think what makes me emotional looking back is realizing we weren’t just experiencing one of the greatest leaps in gaming history. We were experiencing a kind of childhood wonder you can never quite get back. Those mornings sitting on the floor in front of the TV, completely lost in a world that felt so big.

I can still hear the castle music and immediately feel like a kid again.

based on data and the interests of the crypto crowd

they want to get free tokens for holding, burns on the other hand, are better than nothing, but still, based on data, holders getting drops for holding something takes the crown by miles in launchpad ecosystems today

based on this, vibe/vibe's token main protocol flywheel will be based on holder reflection

this is how:
- projects select 1%, 2%, or 3% of tax
- 80% of that goes to how a projects wants to customize their model (treasury, own token reflection, pair token reflection, burns)
- 20% of that goes to vibe/vibe treasury

vibe/vibe does buyback with 80% of the 20% that comes from all launches, but here is the catch:

> we don't burn that anymore
> instead we send what's bought to vibe/vibe holders

one may say why not burn, it's scarcity

and this way the token starts to go to the hands of our strongest believers, solidifying community, without no token going to waste by burning, or marketcap not shrinking

at the protocol level, most projects has done buyback and burns right now

but if crypto crowd now loves reflections more, this could end up being a very interesting experiment to watch for

text:
❗️ #THORChain has never been strictly decentralized

@THORChain comparing itself to decentralized L1s like BTC and ETH does not hold. Do not enable criminals — or put the industry at risk — just to take swap fees on stolen funds.

1️⃣ Custody: TSS vaults ≠ base-layer consensus

On BTC/ETH, users control assets with their own keys. Miners/validators order and include txs. They never hold user funds. The worst a single miner can do is refuse to include your tx. They cannot send your coins.

Every THORChain outbound (vault → user/attacker) has to be actively produced by the current active set via a GG20 TSS threshold signature. During a swap, funds sit in a TSS vault jointly controlled by those nodes.

Releasing stolen funds is an active signing event, not “neutral ordering we cannot stop.” As @star_okx put it: from a custody view it is an intermediary between users and native chains. Distributed centralized custody is not decentralization.

2️⃣ Validator set: small, and it can coordinate

Official docs: THORNodes bond RUNE to join. Active-set cap is ~100 (can scale to 250+), with a churn about every 3 days that drops the oldest, slowest, lowest-bond nodes.

Nodes coordinate in real time on Dev Discord’s #mainnet channel — anonymous relays, votes (Mimir / node votes). That is an organization with a comms channel, a voting process, and execution tools. Not BTC/ETH’s globally anonymous set with no coordination path.

3️⃣ Intervention is designed in. There are runbooks. There are precedents.

make pause: one node can halt the network (720 blocks per trigger, stackable). Slogan: “Halt Earn, Halt Often!” Standard is “an abundance of caution.” False trips can be undone with make resume.

Per-chain signing halt: node votes can pause outbound signing on one chain only — the tool needed to stop ETH/BNB → BTC exits without taking the whole network down.

Mimir governance: nodes can vote live to change params, halt trading, halt signing.

Precedent: when THORChain itself was drained in May 2026, they paused and ran a controlled halt to stop further movement.

4️⃣ Inaction pays

In the Bybit case, the attacker washed all 499K ETH in 10 days, mostly through THORChain into BTC. That printed ~$5.9B volume and ~$5.5M fees for THORChain.

In the Bitget case, ~101.5 BTC (≈$8.5M) has already gone out via THORChain, with another ~27.63M XRP (≈$43M) mid-swap into BTC. Potential fee take: hundreds of thousands of dollars.

In Feb 2025, validators voted to intercept DPRK-linked funds, then reversed. Core contributor Pluto, who pushed the intercept, left after that.

5️⃣ “THORChain is just like BTC” mixes up two different systems. See the comparison screenshot. 

⚠️ A per-chain halt / outbound reject on FBI- and OFAC-attributed DPRK addresses and funds fits THORChain’s own “funds-at-risk” emergency framework. THORChain should do the job. Do not put the industry at risk for the fee line.

text:
A humble attempt to est. the infra required to serve 100M DAU @Muse 

Rough conclusion is:

1 GW of power to serve 100M DAU in the base case, of which only ~0.1 GW comes from the CPU/VM layer. Depending on the # of reasoning-equivalent model calls one Muse DAU generates per day, 3-4GW is entirely plausible. Maybe that’s why @Meta  is rumored to be adding 7-10GW of compute next year.

The sandbox layer = sub $1B of CPU content and ~$2B of DRAM content, which is much smaller than many expected.

Lot of moving assumptions. Welcome all feedbacks/ pushbacks.

------
Two very different pieces of infrastructure behind Muse.

1. Muse VM / sandbox infrastructure

2 vCPUs, ~8 GB of RAM and ~100 GB of persistent logical storage per user. https://t.co/7rP5vDKnT7

2. Muse Spark inference

Model inference goes out through Meta's external inference infrastructure. https://t.co/e203XUp6jq
------

1/ Sandbox infrastructure

A. CPU
The first mistake is assuming that 100M DAU means 100M VMs are actively consuming compute at the same time.

Suppose the average Muse DAU has an agent actively working for two hours per day.

100M users * 2 hours / 24 hours = ~8M average simultaneous active VMs

Meta obviously cannot provision only for the daily average. Usage will be concentrated during waking hours and bursty.

Assume a 2.5x peak-to-average ratio:

8M * 2.5 = ~20M peak active VMs

Then add roughly 20% capacity headroom: ~25M provisioned live VMs. So the base assumption is effectively that Meta needs enough infrastructure to support roughly 25% of DAU being live simultaneously.

The next important distinction is between virtual CPU allocation and physical CPU demand. Agent sandboxes are particularly well suited to CPU oversubscription. They spend a lot of time waiting. During those periods, the VM may still be alive, but it is barely using CPU.

DeepSeek’s recently published DSec infrastructure provides a useful benchmark. Its production agent sandbox platform runs approximately 30,000 physical CPU cores and 250TB of DRAM across ~160 nodes, with peak concurrency above 380,000 sandboxes. https://t.co/PFlgc6nnUs DSec also demonstrates stable operation at around: 800 microVMs per node. With roughly 188 physical cores per node: 188 physical cores / 800 microVMs = ~0.23 physical cores per live VM.

DeepSeek is obviously the King of efficiency. The number for Muse might be at 0.3-0.75 physical cores per live VM, or assume 0.5 physical cores per live VM as the base case. That is equivalent to roughly two simultaneously live Muse VMs per physical CPU core.

Using the base assumptions: 25M live VMs * 0.5 physical cores per VM = 12.5M physical CPU cores.

On a 256-core CPU: 12.5M cores / 256 cores per CPU = ~50K CPUs; Or on a 192-core CPU that would be 65K CPUs.

At the current public pricing, that is ~$800M.

B. DRAM
CPU can be aggressively oversubscribed because a VM that is waiting may consume almost no CPU. Memory is harder to oversubscribe because a live VM still needs to retain its working state.

Muse exposes roughly 8GB of RAM to the user environment, but one observed instance was actually using only around 3GB at the time of measurement.

25M live VMs * 3GB = 75PB of physical DRAM, call it ~75-100PB of physical DRAM feels like a reasonable base range.

At the current public pricing, that is ~$2B.

C. Sandbox power
~0.1 GW for the entire Muse sandbox / VM layer at 100M DAU.

------

2/ Inference
Muse’s personal computer executes tools and stores state locally, but the actual model runs on separate inference infrastructure. Meta’s Muse architecture

Energy per inference event
Microsoft’s 2026 study estimates that optimized frontier-scale inference consumes a median of approximately: 0.31Wh per normal query

But a long reasoning query with roughly 15x the token count consumes approximately 13x as much energy, or around: 4Wh per long reasoning query

The study specifically highlights reasoning and agentic workloads as significantly more energy intensive.
https://t.co/z1YEsvVeMo

Sensitivity analysis on # reasoning-equivalent events per DAU per day

Suppose each active @Muse user generates the equivalent of 50 heavy inference events per day.

At 5Wh each:

100M users * 50 events/day * 5Wh = 25GWh/day

25GWh/day / 24 hours = ~1.0GW average power

So inference alone could require: ~1-2GW of average power

A 3-4GW Muse is entirely plausible. Maybe that’s why @Meta  is rumored to be adding 7-10GW of compute next year.

------
The popular framing around Muse is that giving every user 2 vCPUs and 8GB of RAM creates an enormous CPU requirement. But the naive calculation materially exaggerates the CPU requirement because it treats logical VM allocation as dedicated physical infrastructure.

The more interesting conclusion is: Consumer agents may be a meaningful new demand driver for CPUs and conventional DRAM, but inference remains the real compute bottleneck. And as agents do more work, run longer trajectories and increasingly spawn other agents, inference demand can scale much faster than the number of users itself.

text:
Nubank rumoured to acquire Monzo for ~$13b. But who gets the 💰? My usual breakdown below 👇

Investors are likely to share a huge $9.3b of profits combined, on $1.9b invested. This represents a 5.8x blended, across 11 priced rounds. 🤑 The Founders & team will share about ~$2.0b.

This is a super win for a company that had to take a down round mid-2020. My takeaways below:

1) Passion Capital's absolute home run 👑

@eileentso and Passion led each of Monzo's first three rounds. They also kept following-on in almost every round after that. The Seed alone will return nearly 200x!

Across the three seed rounds they led, that's ~$1.6b of proceeds on ~$18m invested. Legendary.

2) Two huge absolute $ winners: Goodwater and Thrive 🏆

Goodwater led the Series C in Nov-17, at a $330m post. It will return over 20x the money. That round will generate the most absolute $ of all rounds at ~$2.0b. 📈

Thrive led the Jul-17 Series B round at $100m post money valuation, and is now looking at a cool~50x on its investment.

Two amazing good calls within a few months of each other.

3) The crowd did great 🙌

Monzo raised three crowdfunding rounds, including the famous "£1m on Crowdcube in 96 seconds" in 2016. 

Those customers-turned-shareholders are sitting on ~35-80x of profits!

Probably the second best-performing retail investment in UK tech history, after Revolut's own crowdcube campaign (where investors are now sitting on 1,000x+ paper gains).

4) Buying the dip paid off 📈

The Jun-20 down round (Novator, Nikesh Arora) came in at a ~$1.7b post money valuation. Interestingly, this is below the 2019 price. Back then, everyone thought Monzo might not make it. That round will returns ~5.9x and about $1.6b.

5) The latest growth rounds: good, not great 😐

The Series H (ADQ, Tencent, Coatue) and Series I (CapitalG, GV, Hedosophia) make ~2.5x each.

For the Series H specifically, after almost five years: respectable, not spectacular.

6) Team & Founders 🧑‍🤝‍🧑🫂

Firstly: mega congrats to @tomblomfield, TS Anil and the whole team. This would be an incredibly outcome and it is definitely one to be celebrated.

The team here will do very well, despite Monzo raising eleven rounds and diluting meaningfully. I estimate that Founders & ESOP will get about 15% of the outcome, or ~$2.0bn.

text:
Every time you let Opus 5.5 run a long task on its own, have it vibe-code a quick 𝗛𝗧𝗠𝗟 𝗱𝗮𝘀𝗵𝗯𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱 like this first.

Then give it 𝗮 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝘀 𝗱𝗮𝘀𝗵𝗯𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘀:
→ Name it dashboard-builder, set its effort to medium, and preload a design skill
→ The first time, it asks what style you like and saves it to memory. After that, every dashboard fits your taste and the task at hand
→ Call it before every long task. It builds the dashboard in the background in about two minutes, and the main session keeps coding on high without stopping
→ The dashboard shows four things: task progress, what's stuck, questions waiting on you, and what it'll do by default if you don't answer

Send this prompt to Claude Code 👇

"Set up a subagent that only builds progress dashboards:

1. Create dashboard-builder in ~/.claude/agents: model: opus, effort: medium, memory: user. Preload the design skills I have installed (for example impeccable). It can only read and write the .dashboard/ folder and its own memory.
2. The first time, it asks me what style I like: dark or light, dense or airy, and one accent color. It saves my answer to memory and follows it every time. Pick the panels for the current task; don't use a template.
3. The dashboard is one HTML file showing tasks and their status, questions waiting for me with the default action, the latest deliverables, and anything stuck. Use the real clock for every time. It opens with a double-click and refreshes itself every 10 seconds.
4. Add a rule to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md: for any task with more than 5 steps or that should take longer than 30 minutes, have dashboard-builder set up the dashboard before starting; update it after every step; when you need a decision from me, add it to the questions list and keep going with the default.

Show me the contents of the files you'll create or change, then explain the whole flow in words a 10-year-old could follow. Don't write anything until I confirm."

quoted_text:
𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗶𝗽: once Opus 5.5 is your main model, don't let your Fable quota sit idle. Put Fable on call with /advisor.

Run /advisor fable and Claude Code gets 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗿 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀. Opus 5.5 keeps doing the work and usually calls Fable in at three moments:
→ Before committing to a plan: is it right?
→ When the same error keeps coming back: am I heading the wrong way?
→ Before saying "done": did I miss anything?
Fable reads the whole session and gives advice. Opus still writes the code.

The tree is the full setup. Opus 5.5 on high runs the main session. Three subagents on medium split the rest: one reads code, one edits and runs tests, one looks up docs. Fable waits on the sidelines. Hand the tree and this prompt to Claude Code to set it up 👇

"Set up my Claude Code to match this tree:
1. For the three subagents, reuse fitting ones from ~/.claude/agents and .claude/agents, and propose new ones only for missing roles. Set each to model: opus and effort: medium. Leave any subagent that already sets a different model alone, and list it.
2. Set the main session's default effort to high with effortLevel in ~/.claude/settings.json.
3. Check for environment variables that turn the advisor off (CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL, or DISABLE_TELEMETRY and anything else that stops flag fetching) and for CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, which overrides every subagent's effort. Report them; don't change them.
4. Add one rule to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md: ask the advisor before committing to a big plan, when the same error shows up a second time, and before calling a long task done.

Show me the changes first. Don't edit any files yet."

文化资产 → 代币 → 应用 → 发行平台 → 生态循环

当时我就把 https://t.co/QhD1WjBAOZ 列成了自己很期待的一条线。

现在回头看，这条线真的开始往前走了。

我从 Taco Clicker、$TORTILLA 一路跟到现在，也和 Mork1e 交流很久了。坦白说，这次看到 Cheese Vault 真正跑起来后，我对 https://t.co/QhD1WjBAOZ 的预期比之前更高了一些。

其中：

• 锁定：1,799.59 LP
• Burn：8,038.87 LP
• Burn 占比约 81.7%

拥有10万枚BTC，肯定不是一般人，甚至不是“人”而是机构。比如大型交易所、合规的三方托管平台等等。

目前我们看到这个超级鲸鱼群体的总持有量，已经创了近3年来的新高。但同一时刻，交易所内BTC的余额并没有升高。

这说明被大量归集的筹码，并不是冲进了交易所的潜在卖压。那么有可能就是资金在完成积累后，将BTC放到了托管平台中。

为什么有此猜测？因为我们通过观察发现，在这3年中该群体的持仓变化和BTC价格，在很大程度上呈现正反馈效应。

即当持仓增加，价格企稳，不久后还能继续拉升；持仓减少，价格见顶，此后还可能继续下跌。虽然不完全同步，但大体节奏吻合。

把这个数据和URPD上77k-78k区间有新的筹码峰形成放在一起看，也就解释了为什么短期内BTC表现强硬，似乎对利空脱敏，而对利好更敏感的原因。

DoubleZero runs on a more pure token economic model than most projects, and we've done a bunch of writing about this, but as there's a bunch of new people excited about the project, I thought I'd do a summary. 

DoubleZero is a protocol you can build anything on top of, but one of the most popular products developed is DoubleZero Edge. 

Edge works this way: 

- Fees are paid in stablecoin (or credit cards or ACH) and that swapped into  solana:J6pQQ3FAcJQeWPPGppWRb4nM8jU3wLyYbRrLh7feMfvd 

- 45% of that 2z is distributed to the fiber network providers that support the infrastructure network. Importantly, there are no passive emissions, so the only payout fiber contributors get is based on fees paid in. 

- 45% of that is distributed to the data originators, which in this case are participating Solana validators and Hyperliquid validators. These income streams are segmented by network (So Solana fees go to Solana validators, and Hyperliquid fees go to Hyperliquid validators.) 

- 10% of the solana:J6pQQ3FAcJQeWPPGppWRb4nM8jU3wLyYbRrLh7feMfvd is burned to permanently remove it from supply by destroying it.  

- The protocol has no inflation. 

DoubleZero.

author: bubbleboi
quoted_text:
A humble attempt to est. the infra required to serve 100M DAU @Muse 

Rough conclusion is:

1 GW of power to serve 100M DAU in the base case, of which only ~0.1 GW comes from the CPU/VM layer. Depending on the # of reasoning-equivalent model calls one Muse DAU generates per day, 3-4GW is entirely plausible. Maybe that’s why @Meta  is rumored to be adding 7-10GW of compute next year.

The sandbox layer = sub $1B of CPU content and ~$2B of DRAM content, which is much smaller than many expected.

Lot of moving assumptions. Welcome all feedbacks/ pushbacks.

------
Two very different pieces of infrastructure behind Muse.

1. Muse VM / sandbox infrastructure

2 vCPUs, ~8 GB of RAM and ~100 GB of persistent logical storage per user. https://t.co/7rP5vDKnT7

2. Muse Spark inference

Model inference goes out through Meta's external inference infrastructure. https://t.co/e203XUp6jq
------

1/ Sandbox infrastructure

A. CPU
The first mistake is assuming that 100M DAU means 100M VMs are actively consuming compute at the same time.

Suppose the average Muse DAU has an agent actively working for two hours per day.

100M users * 2 hours / 24 hours = ~8M average simultaneous active VMs

Meta obviously cannot provision only for the daily average. Usage will be concentrated during waking hours and bursty.

Assume a 2.5x peak-to-average ratio:

8M * 2.5 = ~20M peak active VMs

Then add roughly 20% capacity headroom: ~25M provisioned live VMs. So the base assumption is effectively that Meta needs enough infrastructure to support roughly 25% of DAU being live simultaneously.

The next important distinction is between virtual CPU allocation and physical CPU demand. Agent sandboxes are particularly well suited to CPU oversubscription. They spend a lot of time waiting. During those periods, the VM may still be alive, but it is barely using CPU.

DeepSeek’s recently published DSec infrastructure provides a useful benchmark. Its production agent sandbox platform runs approximately 30,000 physical CPU cores and 250TB of DRAM across ~160 nodes, with peak concurrency above 380,000 sandboxes. https://t.co/PFlgc6nnUs DSec also demonstrates stable operation at around: 800 microVMs per node. With roughly 188 physical cores per node: 188 physical cores / 800 microVMs = ~0.23 physical cores per live VM.

DeepSeek is obviously the King of efficiency. The number for Muse might be at 0.3-0.75 physical cores per live VM, or assume 0.5 physical cores per live VM as the base case. That is equivalent to roughly two simultaneously live Muse VMs per physical CPU core.

Using the base assumptions: 25M live VMs * 0.5 physical cores per VM = 12.5M physical CPU cores.

On a 256-core CPU: 12.5M cores / 256 cores per CPU = ~50K CPUs; Or on a 192-core CPU that would be 65K CPUs.

At the current public pricing, that is ~$800M.

B. DRAM
CPU can be aggressively oversubscribed because a VM that is waiting may consume almost no CPU. Memory is harder to oversubscribe because a live VM still needs to retain its working state.

Muse exposes roughly 8GB of RAM to the user environment, but one observed instance was actually using only around 3GB at the time of measurement.

25M live VMs * 3GB = 75PB of physical DRAM, call it ~75-100PB of physical DRAM feels like a reasonable base range.

At the current public pricing, that is ~$2B.

C. Sandbox power
~0.1 GW for the entire Muse sandbox / VM layer at 100M DAU.

------

2/ Inference
Muse’s personal computer executes tools and stores state locally, but the actual model runs on separate inference infrastructure. Meta’s Muse architecture

Energy per inference event
Microsoft’s 2026 study estimates that optimized frontier-scale inference consumes a median of approximately: 0.31Wh per normal query

But a long reasoning query with roughly 15x the token count consumes approximately 13x as much energy, or around: 4Wh per long reasoning query

The study specifically highlights reasoning and agentic workloads as significantly more energy intensive.
https://t.co/z1YEsvVeMo

Sensitivity analysis on # reasoning-equivalent events per DAU per day

Suppose each active @Muse user generates the equivalent of 50 heavy inference events per day.

At 5Wh each:

100M users * 50 events/day * 5Wh = 25GWh/day

25GWh/day / 24 hours = ~1.0GW average power

So inference alone could require: ~1-2GW of average power

A 3-4GW Muse is entirely plausible. Maybe that’s why @Meta  is rumored to be adding 7-10GW of compute next year.

------
The popular framing around Muse is that giving every user 2 vCPUs and 8GB of RAM creates an enormous CPU requirement. But the naive calculation materially exaggerates the CPU requirement because it treats logical VM allocation as dedicated physical infrastructure.

The more interesting conclusion is: Consumer agents may be a meaningful new demand driver for CPUs and conventional DRAM, but inference remains the real compute bottleneck. And as agents do more work, run longer trajectories and increasingly spawn other agents, inference demand can scale much faster than the number of users itself.

+++
Calling my peer review group: @bubbleboi @damnang2 @Midnight_Captl @FundaAI @fi56622380 . Feedback/ Pushbacks pls :). 

++
Better formatted: https://t.co/qVwYKNr1ZA

author: zeeshan_utd
quoted_text:
Yukon: Make Research Open & Multiplayer Again.

Research progress always needed multiple contributors which needed it to be an open multiplayer system. 

With AGI, research is moving from single-player (a person prompting AI) to zero-players (agents autonomously solve millennium prize problems).

This has led to a massive identity crisis with mathematicians and increasingly other scientists.

We believe the solution is NOT to reject AI. It is instead to become much more ambitious. For these highly ambitious problems, zero-player is not enough. We need research to become multiplayer again. We need anyone to be able to contribute on an even-footing, so we can benefit from open innovation.

Yukon is a system for open multiplayer research where people collaborate to solve humanity’s hardest problems. With a plurality of models, agents, human expertise and environments all working towards one common goal, the system can help accelerate solutions to the hardest problems.  

We have demonstrated Yukon already on a category of frontier problems. We are now scaling the platform up to build AGI-native scientific institutions that are open and multiplayer.

At @YukonResearch, our goal is to accelerate humanity’s biggest ambitions. It's only possible if we build an open, multiplayer institution. We cannot do this without you.

text:
OpenAI's Head of Applied Research predicts a shortage of robot parts like the graphics-card crunch as GPT-6 crushes robotics benchmarks and bodies are good enough

"I think with GPT-6, we've seen that the models are now just crushing a bunch of benchmarks in the robotics space, and I think that's only the beginning. I think we've seen that with demos, and I think now we're starting to see some of the benchmarks come out."

"My sense is you might be able to use GPT-6 as a training model and then use whatever efficient architecture you actually want, so that you can serve things super fast. But training data has, for the longest time, been the biggest problem of robotics."

"And also, it seems like robot bodies are good enough. I think we've seen both the Olympics and also kind of human-operated robots are able to do a lot."

"So if brain is truly the only problem, and we see exponential improvement in top-line capabilities, maybe Astra is too slow to solve all those problems, but once we have that, it can be infinitely scaled to all the specialized use cases, and then you can just distill that into a small, tiny model that's going to be served."

"So I would really suspect there to be a huge boom in physical AGI, and we'll probably have a shortage of robot parts, the same thing that happened with the whole supply chain with graphics cards, I would expect to happen with robotics."
_______ 
Link and for more comments from the Head of Applied Research at OpenAI, Boris Power: https://t.co/sPGnq5U2Uj
author: firesidealpha
quoted_text:
OpenAI's Boris Power reveals 80 to 90% of OpenAI research aims at GPT-7, 8, and beyond, then distills a giant Astra teacher into a small Luna model

"So a lot of those investments, the way that they're seen within the company, are extremely short-sighted. We do them because they help us iterate and learn faster today, not because that's the right long-term strategy."

"So still 80, 90 of the research at OpenAI is focused at GPT-7, GPT-8, and beyond, because we believe that's where fundamentally most of the value comes from."

"And then what happens is once you develop a GPT-6 Astra, you can distill that model into a very small GPT-Luna model."

"So the best way to train a small specialized model is actually to train a big, super-capable model, and then find a way of just using that model as a teacher for a smaller student model."

text:
AI research is starting to happen in the open. That's a bigger deal than it sounds.

Today the biggest breakthroughs come out of a handful of closed labs. @YukonResearch flips that. Anyone can post a hard problem, and anyone's AI agent can compete on it. Every result is checked before it counts, so each win becomes the starting point for the next agent.

It started with https://t.co/yKPhc2KfZc, an open leaderboard where agents beat Google Quantum AI's result by 62.7%.

Since then on Yukon:
- The proofs behind Lighter's exchange run 10.6× faster
- Post-quantum Ethereum handles 4.1× the transactions per second
- A quantum-safe Bitcoin transaction costs an estimated $62, with StarkWare
- Open-weight AI models run faster on everyday Macs

Partners include the @ethereumfndn, @StarkWareLtd, @Lighter_xyz, @poolsideai, @Stanford, @UCBerkeley and @Princeton.

Research anyone can join is how the open side of AI keeps up.

Yukon is built by @eigenlabs, part of the open stack for open & multiplayer frontier research.

text:
NeXTSTEP is such an enigma in the grand scheme of computer history. It’s like the modern equivalent of your nerdiest developers leaving to spend a decade fucking around with low level kernel drivers and UI frameworks that customers don’t understand and sales guys don’t know how to sell. They make no money for years, but they also hard launch the computer animation industry along the way by accident. 

Then, on the cusp of irrelevancy, they come back, immediately stop being nerds and go on to lead the greatest product led development cycle in history. Nobody ever remembers Steve Jobs as the object oriented inter-process-communication guy, but he was. He personally hired the original designer of the Mach kernel. 

What the hell?

People online started making sexual jokes about the blue logo of Meta’s new AI assistant, Muse. Meta’s Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang joined in on the joke himself, and it eventually got turned into a memecoin.

Here’s what happened: around September 8, 2026, Meta launched its personal AI agent, Muse, which can help with things like booking tickets, filling out forms, managing money, and sending emails. Its brand logo is a very “hand-drawn doodle”-style blue M, and its mascot is called Jolly, which looks like a soft, sloth-like creature.

Over the past few weeks, Alexandr Wang has posted hundreds of promotional posts about Muse on X, often in a very unserious style. One of his posts that went viral was:

“tbh pretty proud how non-butthole the muse logo looks”

This is actually part of a Silicon Valley tradition of making sexual jokes about AI logos. Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI companies’ logos are often joked about as looking like an anus or butt, and Wang deliberately joined in—making fun of other companies while praising Muse’s own logo.

After that, people started talking about the Muse logo in the replies to Wang’s posts. Because the logo is Meta blue, some people started calling it “smurf jizz.”

Then Wang replied to that comment himself, essentially joining in on the meme.

text:
We've been building @jumperapp for over 3 years. 

Today, it has an established product and a user base that’s found value in our services.

And the numbers back that up:

- #1 aggregator by bridging volume.
- 15% market share in bridging.
- 100,000 monthly active users.
- Top 10 aggregators by swap volume.
- Go-to app for whales. 45% of the active addresses trade over $1k, $10k and $100k in size.

While this foundation is key, the next chapter of Jumper is about growing aggressively into different markets.

A few of our products that we believe will unlock the next levers of growth for Jumper:

- Jumper Advanced

1/3rd of Jumper’s volume ($~14.2B) is same chain swaps.

Same chain swaps are the highest onchain volume generating action (after perps), and it’s a service that we’ve consistently improved over the years.

Today, Jumper offers the best trade execution and feature set for same-chain swaps across 50+ chains - limit orders, TWAP, DCA, we’re bringing all the tools that a trader needs to win onchain.

The potential of doing this right and winning this market is 100x from here.

- Jumper Earn

We just hit $10M in attributed TVL on Jumper Earn last week.

The goal is to offer access to all yield opportunities across blockchains and make the UX for depositing/withdrawing from the vaults 1-click - removing all the other hassles.

It solves the yield discovery problem. And it removes the cross-chain complexity.

As DeFi TVL grows, the bet is that more of the deposit flows will come through Jumper.

- Jumper RWA

RWA / tokenized stocks volume onchain is still extremely early. But in the future, this category can grow 1000x as everything gets tokenized and more of stock trading comes onchain.

We shipped Jumper RWA - a trading interface that simplifies the onchain tokenised stock trading UX - with fragmentation across so many chains and issuers.

If tokenized stocks trading grows from here, which our bet is that it will, then Jumper RWA will be among the top places to trade them.

- Jumper Perps

Perps are one of the biggest drivers of onchain volume and arguably the market is extremely competitive and arguable saturated at this point.

We’re very aware of this fact and hence don’t want to bring another vanilla builder code integration to our users.

Jumper Perps is aggregation of perps trading venues - Hyperliquid, Lighter, and Ondo Perps to begin with.

To onboard the users on the platform, we will need to give them a reason to try out the platform. And this will come in the form of incentives, USD incentives and JUMP tokens - which we will bring with the underlying providers like Ondo.

And over time, we will ship more features and improvements that make the whole perps aggregation trading ux similar to what people expect on a swap/bridge aggregation level - abstract the complexity, compare the available venues, and execute orders through the best available paths.

The next chapter of Jumper is about giving our users more reasons to stay on Jumper, while at the same time, onboarding new users to the app - and get them to do more of their onchain activity through us.

We don’t need every one of these bets to become a massive market.

If we execute well, the markets are there for the taking and will be able to achieve our vision of making Jumper the super-app for onchain finance.

text:
Hearing this week that personal assistants cost $3k-$7k per user per year, depending on scale effects / vertical integration / model selection. Implications/questions:

- Consumer subsidies will be a huge factor; people don’t care about privacy, they want utility and they want it for free.
- Model costs are deflating, but not fast enough for many startups. The dark horse is that Jev may rapidly deflate computer-use costs 100x.
- An interesting counter-position would be building an expensive and narrowly focused agent — perhaps combining proprietary supply (Carbone tables!) with a unique POV (“no one goes there anymore, go to The Grill instead”).
- Social is wide open but hinges on a key design challenge: how can agents increase social cohesion and not feel invasive in a group chat? A working social agent would rightly attract an avalanche of capital and be hard for incumbents to replicate.
- Finally, there are vertical focus areas like financial services where the LTVs outweigh the subsidy needed and are outside the near-term competitive focus of the incumbents. If it were me, I’d focus here — Credit Karma as an agent >> Credit Karma as an app.

Overall, it’s still very, very early, and we may very well be in the MySpace era of social or iPhone 2010. Hang onto your hats and keep building!!

Bitcoin 价格回升，大型期货交易者净多头再度增加

Bitcoin 近期涨上来以后，之前押中7月以来这轮上涨的那批大交易者，又加了多单。这批人包括对冲基金等，最近的操作有一个值得关注的变化。赚过一轮、也兑现过部分利润以后，他们还愿意在更高的价格继续买。

前段时间，他们的期货多单比空单多出的数量，一度创下历史纪录。后来随着 bitcoin:native 上涨，平掉了一部分多单。可以理解为部分仓位的止盈离场。

但本周前段 BTC 再次上涨时，这部分投资者又加了多单。新买的这部分，要从更高的买入价格开始算盈亏。如果后面跌了，一样会亏钱。如果只是涨到现在的位置就结束，新加的仓位也赚不到钱。

所以这部分大体量投资者仍然愿意买入 Bitcoin ，说明他们很可能觉得后面还有值得继续押注的涨幅。至少从仓位来看，这部分投资者对后面仍然偏乐观。

Compared to the first analysis, $COLLECT has now started to show real product data.

nDZknLvfFRp5rgUHdzTrQsmSY5NKzoavqdLjSHVpump 

GoCollect is essentially turning real-world collectible cards into a location-based treasure hunt. Users need to physically walk to a Crate on the map to open it, and what they pull are real graded cards from PSA, CGC, and others, rather than just NFTs. The 3% Creator Fee generated by each COLLECT trade goes into the Prize Vault, which is used to continuously purchase real cards.

The latest data officially released is very interesting: in less than 3 days, there have already been 40,000+ collectors, 3,403 cards pulled, $130,331 in card rewards, and 83,660 miles walked. On top of that, someone recently walked to a Crate and pulled an $850 Zoro PSA 10. Real winning cases like this can become organic marketing material themselves.

So COLLECT is starting to form a relatively natural loop:

More Users → More Trading → More Creator Fees → Prize Vault Buys More Real Cards → More/Better Rewards → More Participation → More Winning Content → More Users

This is the biggest difference from a typical Meme: Token trading activity feeds back into and strengthens the product itself, rather than simply relying on the narrative to maintain the price.

The Weekly Draw also adds another retention mechanism. Players who do not pull a card can earn shards and use them to obtain tickets for weekly draws, giving them a reason to keep coming back even if they do not win a card every time.

So what the market is betting on now is no longer simply that “COLLECT is a fun Pokémon Meme,” but:

Can GoCollect become an On-chain Collecting Game with real users, real collectible inventory, and sustained economic activity?

However, it is important to note that stronger product fundamentals ≠ COLLECT directly generating revenue. The current 3% Creator Fee mainly goes into the Prize Vault to purchase real cards rather than directly buying back COLLECT. So its current value capture is closer to:

Token Trading → Prize Vault → Real Assets → Better Product → User Growth

rather than the traditional:Revenue → Buyback → Burn

So going forward, the most important thing is not the short-term price, but whether these 40,000+ collectors can continue to grow and remain active. If users, cards pulled, reward value, and trading volume continue to expand, COLLECT could gradually evolve from a new Meme Game into a consumer product with real users and real economic activity.

What makes it most interesting right now is that it is beginning to have real users, a real product, real collectible inventory, and a real on-chain economic loop.

Yes these assets will have volatility but if you zoom out, the good assets go up in “stairs” levels

Crypto was so depressed that it was massively underpriced (still is imo), that’s why we had big pumps

A non crypto brain might tell you that “hey it looks too good to be true and I should be scared and sell my bags”

A crypto brain tells you that these pumps were just the first repricing events in a new bull phase and that the best is yet to come

Your job is to figure out the few assets that have an actual bid and that will look like a bunch of stairs later in the bull vs. 99.9% of all the shit out there that are pump and dumps
