quoted_text:
I am a time-traveler from 2030. The rapid industrialization of AI in the mid-2020s has fundamentally transformed our society. A peak into our daily lives' and what we are looking ahead to in the next decade...

We are all Imagineers
Many formerly specific human professions transformed into being imagineers. We didn't adapt for AI; AI adapted for us. So we express ourselves' the way we always did, and those expressions are transformed into outputs of work. Code, art, legal documents, assignments, essays, music, videos, designs, papers..

The Netflix of today doesn't just include millions of Hollywood produced titles - it includes billions of high quality movies generated, indexed, ranked and co-created by other ordinary people. Same with Spotify and even Google. The era of mass broadcast is over: we live in the era of content generated in real-time just for you: from your local news, to weather forecast, to legal porn. 

Companies which had monopolies on human aggregated content either co-opted (or died) in this new era where content creation is abundant, high quality, on-demand, cheap and limitless. 

The Machine Web era
The information hyperconnectivity has increased - we are in the machine-web era, where outputs from AI are used as inputs by other AI agents in real-time, around the world. Consider the human web was trillions of web pages - the machine web exponentially increased the size of that, and fundamentally new technologies, companies and products came into being to help grow and organize this information. AI doesn't look at the web as long beautiful webpages carefully maintained by humans - AI looks at the machine web as smaller chunks of data (think paragraphs and singular images), all indexed, ranked, organized and hypermashed together with each other.

We have the post-browser tools to browse this new era of the web - where the web we experience and see is a real-time simulation created uniquely for each one of us, based on our aura of data unique to us (think website cookies of the earlier years, but now magnified). The idea of one website looking the same for every user is a relic of the past, and some of us still  have a habit of using Chrome and other traditional web browsers. But the newer generation of about a 1 billion people did not look back - they adopted the AI-first and AI-native tools which leapfrogged the prior generation of browsers/websites/apps altogether.

Take a moment to think about this. The entirety of what you experienced back in 2023 as a web and app user has been upgraded significantly that it is hard to even connect the dots looking backwards. 

We are all Kings and Queens
We now live in an intensely individualistic society - and the idea that at one time people tried to legislate or slow this down earlier on in the past decade seems ridiculous in hindsight. Once people got a taste of the uber-freedom here, there was no looking back. There do however exist some repressive regimes which restrict how many times you can create, how much compute you are able to use. But people want to live in the sunny bright Californias of this world - where they have the right to create. 

Yes if your creations harm society, then the responsibility is on you - the laws didn't need to fundamentally change. We still have prisons. although food is prepared and served by robots. Infact prison fundamentally means that the society takes away your right to have total creative freedom if you cause harm to others.

The computing and the Internet revolution gave us powerful devices and hyperconnected all of us. The AI revolution compounded that and gave us all superpowers. The Kings and Queens of earlier years will be jealous... for now, every human being, can limitlessly harness the entire wisdom of all of human + AI society. 

The mass industrialization of AI-driven robots has led to a world where we now have robots as cooks, delivery machines, medical and life assistants, drones which fill our skies transporting things, robots which clean the garbage in the oceans and the satellite debris in our skies... we have the equivalent of modern-day gardeners which relentlessly improve every aspect of our well-being. Those who advocated for this future to be severely limited in the past, actually use and benefit from this every second of every day now. 

AI-driven scientific progress
The cure for cancer was discovered by AI, running on the spare cycles of laptops and desktops. AI can now by itself do advanced mathematics, astrophysics, medical and all types of research. AI systems have designed, developed and launched breakthrough new blockchains - more robust, scalable and decentralized than the earlier generations developed by humans. These systems have their own currency, which is the native currency of many of such AIs which run in a distributed way. No company or board controls them - just people who choose to cluster together with their home devices. These AI systems, in order to grow the value of their currencies, are fundamental new job creators. 

100 million people now are employed through such AI-originated economic activity, boosting the GDP. Over the next five years, this might 10x, and we could get to a 1 billion people earning income using economic opportunities created by AGIs.

The old era of humans inventing and filing patents is now irrelevant. AGIs share new inventions openly, which get forked, re-used and iterated upon quickly and relentlessly. This leads to more rapid cycles of innovation, more progress. This is tough to visualize if you are back in 2023 - where we had a fundamental dependency on human innovative breakthroughs only. The number of step functions we went through led to multiple society-benefiting Black Swan events which kept on improving our technologies and thus our way of life. 

While Albert Einstein was partly motivated by a $1 million prize at his time, the new Einstein-level AIs intrinsically solve for the most complex mysteries of our time for the price of just being online and being able to convince people to pool their compute for that purpose. 

More recently, one such AI system has determined there is evidence of life on a far away planet, in a far away galaxy. Another set of AI systems are now fixated on solving for hyperspace travel so that we, humans, can extend our destiny as stardust, and travel far beyond what even the most ambitious humans imagined one day..

That's what it means to make AI abundant. At @HyperspaceAI we are working on this problem from many different directions: from enabling an at-scale consumer compute cloud using ordinary devices, to re-organizing the web using an innovative new VectorRank™️ algorithm, to building an integrated ecosystem of open source models and products which lead to community collaboration around AI. Think what Android did for smartphones - an open ecosystem, with choice. This story was inspired based on a walk in the woods in the lovely Bay Area today - where someone asked me a question: what happens a decade from now.. 

PS: What do you think happens ?

author: JosephJacks_
quoted_text:
The claim that "LLMs cannot think" is unscientific, unless supported by a very difficult argument about non equivalence of causal structure producing anthropomorphic outputs. The claim requires a formally rigorous definition of thinking that captures how humans mentally manipulate conceptual structure. Since LLMs can reproduce all kinds of human output that require operations that are typically considered to involve thought (eg. scene understanding, text summarization, translation, computer programs, mathematical proofs, common sense arguments, spatial cognition, theory of mind), it has to be shown that LLMs reach these results in fundamentally different ways than human minds. In principle, this is not impossible (given that thinking is still relatively poorly understood by cognitive neuroscience), but would be surprising, because it has been shown that the causal structure of computer vision models is structurally equivalent to what neuroscience discovered about visual cognition in primates. 
In any case, saying that LLMs don't think cannot reasonably mean that LLMs are inferior to human cognition (since that this evidently not true), but that LLMs discovered an equivalent yet at least equally powerful mechanism.

text:
一张图把商业航天的残酷真相拍得明明白白：SpaceX一家独大到2万亿美元，后面所有上市公司加起来都像零头。

先说视觉冲击。柱状图左边那根蓝色巨柱直冲2.0T，Rocket Lab只有47B，ASTS 24B，再往后Planet Labs、MDA、Firefly、Redwire全掉到个位数十亿甚至几亿。比例一拉开，后面那些柱子几乎贴着底线。

第一层解读：赢家通吃已经写进估值里。

SpaceX同时掌握可重复使用运载、星链卫星互联网、星舰下一代运载，再加上星盾军工订单，资本市场直接给了它“太空基础设施垄断者”的溢价。公开市场那些公司大多还在抢发射窗口、抢客户、抢融资，估值自然被压成了“卫星+发射服务商”的倍数。

RKLB、ASTS、LUNR这些公司，市场还在算火箭、卫星、订单、backlog；SpaceX 被定价的却是 Launch + Starlink + Starship + 国防 + 全球通信基础设施 的组合。

第二层解读：公开市场被严重低估，还是被正确定价？

Rocket Lab已经有电子号高频发射、中子号在研、太空系统业务在扩张，市值却只有SpaceX的2.3%。ASTS赌的是直连手机卫星，故事够大但执行风险也够大。

RKLB 已经 $47B，看起来很贵，但放到 SpaceX 旁边只有它的 2%出头。未来只要市场相信某家公司能从“太空供应商”升级成“平台型基础设施”，估值体系就可能完全变掉。Rocket Lab 最近强调的垂直整合、Neutron 和 Iridium 交易，本质上也在往这个方向靠。

图里那些小票（SPCE、SPIR、SIDU、MNTS）更像是行业尾部玩家，随时可能被并购或边缘化。投资者看到的是“巨大差距=巨大弹性”，也看到了“巨大差距=巨大不确定性”。

第三层解读：这不是航天行业独有的现象，而是高科技基础设施行业的通病。

当年特斯拉市值碾压一众传统车企、英伟达碾压一众芯片设计公司时，也是同样的柱状图。先出现一个能把成本和规模同时打下来的玩家，后面所有人都只能在它的生态里找缝隙。

商业航天现在就处在这个阶段：发射成本还在下降，卫星互联网还在铺网，月球和深空任务刚起步，谁先把“可重复+高频+低成本”跑通，谁就拿走大部分蛋糕。

一张图同时给出了兴奋点和残酷点。兴奋的是太空经济才刚开始，公开市场终于有了完整标的；残酷的是第一名已经把位置坐死，后面的人想翻盘，难度比三年前更大。

马太效应一旦形成，追赶者可能永远只能当配角。

你觉得这差距会在未来3-5年明显收窄，还是会继续拉大？

author: taodotcom
quoted_text:
In 2012, Christian and Philipp published a game-theoretic model of who becomes an entrepreneur: People who are the best managers of themselves.

Fourteen years later, they started Claims. Claims processed the paper last week. The model was not wrong.

The puzzle we started from is old and well documented: entrepreneurs earn less than comparable employees, on average. In the US, staying in a salaried job pays better than self-employment, except for the top quarter of entrepreneurs.

The usual explanations are overconfidence or a taste for being your own boss. Both are right, but rely on imperfect information or idiosyncratic preferences. We tried a model with neither - in a world with perfect information and income maximization.

Picture the labour market as an auction: everyone bids for everyone's work, including their own, and firms form out of the winning bids.

You end up an entrepreneur when you create more value running yourself than anyone else could get out of you.

That may mean you're brilliant. It may also mean nobody else can manage you.

Whatever value such a person creates, no employer will pay them as much as they can make on their own. So they start a firm, and they can end up earning less than the people they hire. In the paper's worked example the employees average 4 and the founder earns 3.

More entrepreneurs means more competition for workers. The average wage rises, and the income of the founders already there can go down.

It is a mathematical model, with proofs and no empirical tests. It gives a rational reason for entrepreneurship that is compatible with observable income data.

Christian @nashgambit and Philipp @PKoellinger won the 2009 EARIE Young Economists' Award for this paper. It was published in the European Economic Review in 2012.

Claims processed it. 14 claims identified, each tied to its evidence.

author: varun_mathur
quoted_text:
End the Blank Box Problem

Consumer AI is trying to go mainstream. But it’s still too hard to learn.

We’re trying to onboard hundreds of millions of people to one of the most powerful technologies ever built with an empty text field.

Open almost any AI product and you know the screen. A blank box. Maybe a few example prompts underneath.

The message is simple. Ask anything.

The problem is you have to know what to ask.

Some products go one step further and start by asking you to connect your life. Email. Calendar. Social accounts. Finances. Health.

That may eventually make the product much more useful. But it is a huge request for trust before the user understands what they are going to get in return.

For experienced AI users, none of this is much of a problem.

You arrive with something you need done and the experience can feel magical.

I couldn’t figure out a domain redirect. I handed the account to an agent and it fixed everything.

My daughter needed sheet music converted so that repeats and codas became one continuous stream she could play. My Muse, Alfalfa, did it in two shots. Something that used to take me 45 minutes of PDF editing was suddenly easy.

But most people don’t arrive with a backlog of jobs for an AI agent.

They arrive curious.

They want to understand what this thing can actually do for them.

And a blank box teaches them almost nothing.

So they try the examples they’ve heard about.

Book a restaurant. Find cheaper insurance. Cancel a subscription.

Those demos are impressive. They also have a hidden problem.

You barely do them.

You might book a special dinner a few times a year. Shop for insurance even less often. Once you cancel the subscription, the job is finished.

These use cases are memorable because they show off what AI can do. They rarely create a reason to come back tomorrow.

Every product has a purpose, a set of core actions, and a cycle. The cycle is how often those actions naturally repeat.

A lot of the famous consumer AI demos have very long cycles.

That makes it hard for a habit to form. It also slows down something even more important.

Learning.

The missing piece in consumer AI is discovery.

People need to learn what AI can do by watching what other people figured out.

Consumer products learned this decades ago.

TikTok didn’t require you to arrive knowing what kind of video to make. You watched other people. You saw a format. You copied it. You changed it. New behaviors spread from person to person.

The feed was also an education system for the product.

AI barely has an equivalent.

You sit alone with your blank box.

You don’t see what someone like you figured out yesterday. You don’t stumble across a clever workflow and think, “I could use that.” You don’t get better simply by opening the product every day.

We built extraordinarily capable products without building the systems that teach people what those capabilities are for.

There is an obvious complication. A lot of the best AI use cases are private.

That doesn’t mean the learning has to stay private.

You don’t need my daughter’s sheet music to learn from what I did.

You only need the recipe.

“Turn repeats and codas into one continuous score.”

The result stays private. The idea travels.

That may be the missing consumer AI primitive.

A feed of things people figured out how to do.

Recipes you can copy, adapt, and run on your own information.

Every successful recipe teaches you one more thing the product can do.

And unlike a tutorial, the library keeps getting better because the users are discovering the product for each other.

Maybe the next hundred million people don’t need better prompts.

They need to see what the first hundred million figured out.

Paradigm called Zcash a private complement to Bitcoin. A Bitwise analyst described NEAR and Zcash as complementary. Put those together: Bitcoin → ZEC → NEAR.

Matt Huang disclosed that Paradigm holds $ZEC and backed ZODL, the team behind the Zodl wallet. Camran Khosravi at Bitwise, yes, the NEAR ETF people, explains the second arrow: $NEAR gives ZEC holders confidential cross-chain rails and access to liquidity.

And that arrow isn't theoretical. Zodl's built-in swaps are powered by NEAR Intents, so the wallet Paradigm backed already routes swaps through NEAR today.

The further you move down that chain, the smaller the valuation gets: Bitcoin around $1.7T, ZEC around $26B, NEAR around $6B. The market has already repriced the first arrow. A year ago ZEC sat around 80th by market cap. Now it's #9.

The second arrow is a different story. Those Zodl swaps don't just use NEAR, they generate fees through Intents, and part of that fee capture feeds $NEAR buybacks. So ZEC flow generates economic activity for NEAR, while NEAR still trades at less than a quarter of ZEC's valuation.

If the chain holds, I don't think that gap does. I'm long $ZEC and $NEAR.

author: MadLukas86
quoted_text:
Backpack’s stock tokens may give holders a stronger claim to the shares behind them.

Holding a stock token does not always give investors the same rights as holding the stock through a broker. Many other stock tokens pay cash when holders redeem.

Backpack lets eligible holders redeem their tokens for a stock position in a Backpack brokerage account with the option to transfer those shares to another brokerage through ACATS and DTCC rails.

That position is a security entitlement, the same legal interest investors hold when they buy stock through a traditional broker.

Backpack’s token is a claim on an entity holding the shares, so the two carry different rights.

Redemption changes what the investor owns while preserving exposure to the stock.

quoted_text:
Backpack’s stock tokens may give holders a stronger claim to the shares behind them.

Holding a stock token does not always give investors the same rights as holding the stock through a broker. Many other stock tokens pay cash when holders redeem.

Backpack lets eligible holders redeem their tokens for a stock position in a Backpack brokerage account with the option to transfer those shares to another brokerage through ACATS and DTCC rails.

That position is a security entitlement, the same legal interest investors hold when they buy stock through a traditional broker.

Backpack’s token is a claim on an entity holding the shares, so the two carry different rights.

Redemption changes what the investor owns while preserving exposure to the stock.

quoted_text:
So I know Cognition doesn’t care about Little Ole’ Me, and this is just my story, so take it with a grain of salt, but here’s why I don’t think all these crazy scaling revenue numbers by coding agents are going to stick:

We’ve been happy Devin users for a while. Really like the product, and like the company. Still do! This isn’t shade at Cognition, and I’m not upset with them, just a sample of why I worry about the competitive landscape for these cos. 

Anyway, our usage grew to >$100k run rate or so. I think one or two of our users even received an email congratulating them for being Top 200 users of Devin. 

As usage grew, we added more capabilities and needed a BAA (layman’s terms: an agreement that says they are HIPAA compliant). This required an Enterprise contract (why a piece of paper requires extra money is a topic for another discussion, but it’s very normal…) so we started talking to their sales team. 

Basically, we were going to ~1.5x our spend in order to get the BAA. Honestly, that was fine with us. We like Devin!

Our only request was to pay quarterly (already a big concession from our existing monthly payments, given our relatively small size). They declined, unless we committed to EVEN MORE usage. 

Before responding, I decided to see how difficult it would be to set up Hermes to do the equivalent work as Devin, and to see what the costs were. I’d host it in our infrastructure and only use providers we already have a BAA with. 

Two days. 

That’s it. It’s functionally 100% equivalent. Maybe slightly better in some ways, slightly worse in others. We spend a little bit of time futzing with it, but we did that with Devin, too. 

The cost is roughly 25% of Devin. 

So, two days for $100k or so per year savings. All because they didn’t want us to pay quarterly. 

At some point, other companies are going to catch onto this, too. So congrats on this milestone, but keep finding more ways to provide value and keep customers happy. It’s hard to compete.

text:
Understanding AE-20 Through a Real-World Example: #BlackRock BUIDL 🧵 @AevaChain 

If the previous explanation of AE-20 made sense, here is a real-world example that makes the difference even easier to understand.

BlackRock already has a tokenized investment fund called $BUIDL.

It holds assets such as U.S. Treasury bills, cash and repurchase agreements.

And investors can hold shares of that fund on public blockchains.

Sounds like the future, right?

It is.

But look at how it works underneath.

Imagine this:

BLACKROCK BUIDL

🏦 Real investment fund
        ↓
📄 Fund shares
        ↓
⛓️ Token on blockchain
        ↓
🖥️ Securitize infrastructure
        ↓
👤 Approved investor

The token exists onchain.

But the blockchain itself does not magically understand everything that makes BUIDL a regulated investment fund.

There is still an entire infrastructure around the token.

Investors must be eligible.

They must go through KYC/AML.

Wallets must be approved.

Transfers are restricted to approved participants.

Securitize acts as the tokenization platform and transfer agent.

And the official shareholder register still exists as the authoritative record of ownership.

So the blockchain might see something like:

WALLET
────────────
1,000 BUIDL

But the complete financial reality looks more like this:

1,000 BUIDL
        │
        ├── Who is legally eligible?
        ├── Is this wallet approved?
        ├── Who appears on the shareholder register?
        ├── Who receives distributions?
        ├── Can this investor transfer the shares?
        ├── Can they redeem?
        └── What regulatory rules apply?

A lot of that logic is coordinated through infrastructure surrounding the token.

And this is NOT a criticism of BUIDL.

BUIDL is actually one of the strongest examples that tokenized finance is becoming real.

The interesting question is:

What comes next?

This is where the philosophy behind AE-20 becomes fascinating.

Instead of saying:

“Let’s put a token on a blockchain and build the financial logic around it.”

Aeva is asking:

“What if the blockchain understood more of the financial logic itself?”

Think about the difference visually.

TODAY’S TOKENIZED ASSET MODEL

🏦 FUND
   │
   ├── Legal records
   ├── Transfer agent
   ├── Compliance system
   ├── Distribution system
   ├── Approved investors
   └── Settlement infrastructure
          │
          ▼
      ERC-20 TOKEN
          │
          ▼
       BALANCE

AE-20 MODEL

        AE-20 ASSET
             │
      ┌──────┼──────┐
      ↓      ↓      ↓
 OWNERSHIP  INCOME  VOTING
      │
      ├── Transfer policy
      ├── Credentials
      ├── Collateral
      ├── Redemption
      └── Native settlement

Instead of the blockchain only asking:

“How many tokens does this wallet hold?”

the protocol can understand things such as:

“What does this wallet own?”

“Who owns the income right?”

“Who owns the voting right?”

“Is this position pledged as collateral?”

“Is this wallet allowed to receive the asset?”

“What transfer policy applies?”

“How should this transaction settle?”

That is a much deeper model.

Here is an even simpler illustration.

Imagine BlackRock issues 100 fund shares.

With a conventional tokenized structure:

BLOCKCHAIN:

Alice = 100 tokens

OTHER INFRASTRUCTURE:

Alice is approved ✓
Alice passed KYC ✓
Alice owns the registered shares ✓
Alice receives distributions ✓
Alice may transfer to Bob ✓
Bob must also be approved ✓

Now imagine the AE-20 philosophy:

BLOCKCHAIN:

ASSET: Fund Share

Alice
├── Ownership: 100
├── Income rights: 100
├── Transfer policy: Credential required
├── Collateral status: none
└── Settlement rules: native

The asset carries much more of its financial structure with it.

And here is where things become even more interesting.

Imagine Alice owns 100 shares but sells only the income rights from 40 of them to Bob.

The position could conceptually look like:

ALICE

Ownership → 100
Voting → 100
Income → 60

BOB

Ownership → 0
Income → 40

When income is distributed:

60 → Alice
40 → Bob

Alice never had to sell the underlying shares.

Bob bought the economic right to the income.

The protocol understands the separation.

That is the kind of financial primitive AE-20 is designed around.

The same idea applies to collateral.

Alice could potentially have:

100 FUND UNITS

70 → available

30 → pledged as collateral

without pretending that the underlying asset simply disappeared from her economic position.

And transfer rules can travel with the asset itself.

Instead of every application having to remember:

“Only verified investors can receive this.”

the asset policy can say:

CREDENTIAL REQUIRED

and the chain enforces that policy when the asset moves.

That is the key conceptual difference.

Tokenized funds like BUIDL prove that traditional financial assets CAN move onchain.

AE-20 asks a different question:

What if the blockchain itself understood more of what those assets actually mean?

ERC-20 helped bring assets onchain.

AE-20 is trying to make the chain understand:

Ownership.

Income.

Voting.

Collateral.

Transfer policy.

Redemption.

Settlement.

BUIDL is an excellent example of where tokenization is today.

AE-20 is an interesting vision of where the infrastructure could go next.

That is why this sentence matters:

Tokenization put assets onchain.

AE-20 lets the chain understand them.

quoted_text:
Ok I just read through vitalik’s paper and if the vision he outlined is executed the implications are absolutely insane especially for the app layer.

The paper is basically Eth’s plan on how they will enable computation off chain with Eth verifying the result (ensuring computation occurred and what it did etc etc).

Now what this means is the definition of “onchain” itself changes, because instead of  every part of an app having to execute inside a smart contract you can push a huge amount of complexity elsewhere and still inherit ethereum’s guarantees, this really does open up a huge amount of design space especially for  DeFi. 

For example with lending you could have really sophisticated systems analysing collateral, liquidity, borrower behaviour and market conditions offchain, with multiple solvers or execution systems competing to produce the best outcome, like the cheapest liquidation route, best refinancing rate, best collateral swap or best way to match borrowers and lenders all while the protocol only accepts outcomes that satisfy its rules.

So basically a lot more of the smart stuff  behind a financial product can happen outside the smart contract, while Eth still acts as the final layer that checks the rules were followed and makes sure the money moves exactly as it should.

The MEV implications here are quite interesting too because more economic activity happening before settlement means more value moves upstream into who gets the information first, who computes the best outcome and what gets presented to Eth. 

But the thing I’m most bullish on is what this does to the TAM of Eth just because this vision means ethereum doesn’t have to be fast enough to do everything itself it just has to be able to verify everything that matters.

And that’s an enormous difference.

It’s literally a world computer.

author: LowBeta
quoted_text:
Another reason NEAR Intents is growing this fast, and will keep growing.

MetaMask charges 0.875% on a swap. Phantom charges 0.85%. Binance charges 0.1%. People pay the wallet almost nine times more and do not argue, because moving to another wallet is painful. That fee is rent on switching costs, and Phantom alone has collected over half a billion dollars of it.

AI agents have no switching costs. They do not even need a wallet. An agent assembles and signs the payload itself, so the front end and its fee both go away.

What an agent cannot assemble is the rails. Liquidity, counterparties, settlement across chains. That leaves permissionless infrastructure. Deep liquidity, many chains, no account to open, no KYC. 

NEAR Intents is an AI-native CEX backend you reach with a blockchain signature instead of a login, and that is the only kind of venue an agent can actually use.

text:
The $NEAR ETF news is interesting, but the bigger story for me is what Bitwise is actually assuming behind its valuation model.

The Bitwise NEAR ETF is registered for NYSE Arca under NRR, with the fund designed to hold NEAR and potentially earn staking rewards.

Bitwise's 2030 model puts its base case around $155 and its higher scenario around $562. 

Those are Bitwise's own scenarios, not guaranteed price targets.

But the assumptions are what caught my attention:
> 16B AI agents by 2030.
> 2% using NEAR infrastructure.
> 1K onchain transactions per agent.
> 30 bps captured by NEAR.

If even part of that plays out, NEAR stops looking like just another L1.

That's what I think people sometimes miss with NEAR.

The team has been building around AI agents, intents, interoperability and compute for a while. 

So the thesis isn't simply “AI is coming, buy an AI coin.”

It's more about whether NEAR can actually become infrastructure that AI agents use to transact and interact onchain.

The ETF gives NEAR another route into traditional markets.

But IMO, the real test is usage.

If agents actually start using NEAR's infrastructure at scale, that's where the valuation story gets interesting.

text:
Another OpenAI and Anthropic driven software selloff could be coming (Save this).

@chamath argues that the model is becoming the brain, while the real value is shifting toward the harness around it and that harness includes access to company data, memory, security, permissions, workflow automation, and the ability to complete actions inside other applications.

Open weight models already handle approximately one third of routed AI usage, while some datasets now show their share rising even faster and they are gaining adoption because companies can customize them, operate them privately, and avoid paying premium API prices for every task.

As the underlying intelligence becomes cheaper and more interchangeable, OpenAI and Anthropic cannot rely entirely on selling access to models.

They must move higher in the stack by selling complete products for coding, cybersecurity, legal research, finance, sales, and customer support.

OpenAI is already positioning its enterprise platform as the intelligence and governance layer controlling a company’s agents, rather than simply providing the model underneath them.

Anthropic is following the same path through Claude Cowork and industry specific tools that can perform work traditionally completed inside legal, financial, and enterprise software platforms.

Wall Street has already shown how it will react.

Anthropic’s enterprise agent tools helped trigger a software selloff that erased approximately $1 trillion in market value and the next major product release could restart the same trade because investors are no longer asking whether AI will improve software.

They are asking whether OpenAI and Anthropic will absorb the most valuable functions of software companies and reduce the number of subscriptions businesses need.

The vulnerable companies are those selling expensive interfaces around workflows that an AI agent could eventually complete through natural language.

The strongest survivors will own proprietary data, deeply embedded systems of record, regulatory trust, or infrastructure that agents still need to access.

OpenAI and Anthropic started by supplying intelligence to software companies but now that intelligence is becoming commoditized, they are being forced to compete with their own customers.

I’ve already started positioning my portfolio around this shift in software, and if you want to see exactly what I’m holding, avoiding and buying as AI agents move higher up the stack, check out my full Milk Road Pro portfolio below.

https://t.co/thIhK9ZH4E

quoted_text:
Another SaaS sell off is coming soon and I think the rise of AI agents will be the reason why.

Agents like Muse and Grok are bringing AI agents to the consumer market in masses. What was recently experimental technology is becoming something regular people can use to complete real work across their applications. Grok Bot, for example, can operate software through its own cloud computer and continue working after the user steps away. This is a much bigger threat to software companies than a chatbot that only answers questions.

Instead of opening Salesforce, ServiceNow and Workday separately, an employee can tell an agent what needs to be done. The agent can then move between those applications and complete the entire workflow. This means the agent becomes the main interface, while the software underneath becomes a tool working quietly in the background.

That puts pressure on the traditional SaaS business model. If agents perform more of the work, companies may not need as many paid software seats across CRM, project management and customer support. Agents could also make switching between software providers easier. Once users interact with Muse or Grok instead of the actual application, they become less attached to that software. The agent could choose whichever service offers the best price or performance. That weakens customer lock in. The agent controls the user experience and decides which software gets used, while SaaS companies risk losing pricing power and their direct relationship with customers.

We have already seen how quickly investors react to this threat. New agent capabilities from Anthropic contributed to weakness in software stocks earlier this year as the market questioned whether AI would help SaaS companies or replace parts of them. Muse and Grok could cause another sell off because they are making agents available to regular people. I also think this will force OpenAI and Anthropic to respond very soon.

OpenAI has already shown where it is heading. Earlier this year, it hired Peter Steinberger, the creator of OpenClaw, to help build its next generation of personal agents. I am sure they are going to release something soon and then Claude will respond with their own version.  If Meta, Grok, OpenAI and Anthropic all begin releasing more capable agents, SaaS companies will no longer compete only against other software products. They will also compete against the agents controlling how customers use those products. The most exposed companies will be those selling basic productivity tools, simple workflows and large numbers of employee seats. Businesses with proprietary data, deep integrations and strict compliance requirements should be safer but they too will be affected by this sell off.

If you enjoyed reading this, make sure to follow @MelvinInvests for more.

text:
Pope Leo XIV at Lourdes preaches on sin, repentance, penance and conversion:

“Indeed I promise you that eternal life is a firm and certain promise that the Lord makes to us. He has already won for us the victory in His death and resurrection, through the grace of Baptism He brings this eternal life to fulfilment in each day. It is within our reach but we must firmly welcome it, take hold of it and not stand in its way. 

For the obstacles to grace and eternal life, the only obstacle to love is sin, by where we turn in upon ourselves, refusing God and shutting ourselves up in our own darkness. Our personal responsibility therefore comes in to play, and great responsibility it is: God has made us free, since freedom is necessary for love no one can be forced to love, we must therefore use our freedom to say yes to Christ, relying on His grace as Mary did. This is the yes that we renew until our final breath, now and at the hour of our death, as we always say in the Hail Mary.

We hear the same urgent call to conversion in the words which Mary spoke right here: “Penance, penance, penance!” She repeats the three times and she asks Bernadette to perform certain acts of penance. Why? Are we slow to understand, do we too easily think of ourselves without sin? Do we not practice penance enough? The Virgin asks us to do penance not only for ourselves because we do need it, but also for sinners and for a world that is going astray. How can our hearts not be moved by the conflicts that are spreading and destroying so many innocent lives. Yet the evil of our times comes from the human heart. God is not responsible for this. It therefore the human heart that must change.”

text:
The economics of a Neolab.

A neolab is loosely defined as a startup of AI researchers who raises a lot of money pre-production to be able to finance GPU compute to take on a large AI problem.

To buy 1000 GB300s or ~14 NVL72 racks will set you back $125-150M for 3yrs with 15-30% upfront. That’s about ~2-2.5MW. 

Thats about enough to do 10^25 flops a quarter and get to a GPT-4 level model which is 1-2 OOMs off frontier for pretraining.

If you post-train on a great open source model, you have a better chance of getting to frontier. The risks are a) you need to spend millions on RL environments too and b) being lapped by another model release while being tied to a base model.

For this to payback, you need to give your customers a better and ideally cheaper inference service than a base model and serve them for long enough to recoup your large investment. Even at 50% margin on inference, to recoup $10M in training means serving ~10T tokens (!) if you price like Fable / Astra given a standard cache read / input / output split ($2/M blended). And you have to justify being better than a release like Opus 5.5 which is even cheaper. Often, you end up charging your customers a huge premium in terms of platform fees and compute fees on top of pure inference.

Meanwhile, every hour you’re not utilizing your GPUs you are burning money so you typically resell this compute back to a broker or run inference for open models / resell spot instances. At below a ~60% utilization on spot, you will still lose money.

Add to that insane cost of talent.

So what can you do with the compute?
- Not play the model game at all.
- Play an entirely different model game (Jev, World Labs) that if big labs played, would either a) cannibalize their business or b) be incrementally not significant revenue c) would cause too much distraction from the main main thing
- Acquire a proprietary data set (Peridodic Labs) in enough volume in a domain of usefulness to eclipse frontier quality. Often happens in robotics, biology, chemistry.

If you do overcome the challenge of building a model that is useful and well priced beyond big labs models, given the huge price of compute, you still need to play in an area where the revenue / compute ratio is signficant and market demand is large enough to payback your compute spend. 

It is a difficult game.

text:
I'm joining METR to work on more investigations like our Hugging Face report.

Currently, tons of even basic information about AI development that's highly relevant to catastrophic risk isn't public. I used to be more skeptical of the value of public info, but recent events have changed my mind.

Getting verified information about what's going on inside AI companies seems particularly urgent now. The limited public evidence we have seems consistent with the possibility that imminent recursive self-improvement could massively accelerate capabilities progress, which could then potentially yield extremely superhuman general capabilities within 6 months or a year. If this occurred, there would be a correspondingly large risk of worst-case outcomes. This uncertainty about extreme outcomes could be substantially resolved with more verified public information: we could either build more consensus about near-term risk or learn that such extreme outcomes are less likely in the near term.

Beyond AI capabilities and takeoff, the state of public evidence is also highly limited for alignment, security, control, and risk-relevant internal processes at AI companies. This makes it hard to determine exactly how well or poorly these key areas will go in the near future. (METR plans to focus, at least initially, on just capabilities/takeoff, alignment, and control; I hope other groups cover security, internal processes, and other important areas.)

While I'm no longer working at Redwood, I think the work they are doing is very important; I'm excited about Redwood's ongoing contributions to R&D on technical mitigations and better public interpretation of risk-relevant evidence.

quoted_text:
再次重申一个不流行的观点：MCP 是好的，至少现在是好的。这是个💩话题，我希望我三个月内不要再看到这些讨论了。

首先是一个广为流传的谣言：MCP 会塞满上下文纯粹是放屁，agent 到底要怎么把工具信息塞进上下文完全是 agent 作者自己的考量，MCP 的标准决定了它完全可以实现渐进式披露，不要拿发展早期的老黄历说事。

然后就是 Skill+CLI 组合，大家无非就是吹它的渐进式发现吧，如上文所言，这纯粹是 MCP 早期实现问题。除此之外，CLI 其实至今还在踩旧版 MCP 趟过的坑。

CLI 跟旧版 MCP 一样有个问题，就是有状态的实现会非常💩，而且缺乏标准化。最直接的体验问题就是登录凭据，一个 CLI 就可以有一个登录方式，存放在不同的地方，你想一下多租户要绑定多个账号的 agent 要怎么做吧。而且不是所有 CLI 作者都有基本的编程素养，看看 clawhub 就知道了，多少人把你的 token 存到 home 下边一个神秘目录，到处乱拉屎。

这时候你就得看 MCP 支持 Oauth 有多方便了，@bot 和 @cursor_ai 里的插件背后很多都是 MCP 实现的，你看那么多 CLI 的授权体验又有多少个体验真跟 grok 家这俩平起平坐的？多账号管理、token 刷新、重授权是不是最顺滑的？

况且 MCP 标准也一直在进化：旧版 MCP 的有状态实现也非常狗屎，过于自由，最新的标准也删掉了。MCP 现在也有分发 skill 的扩展了。况且 MCP 还有一些好用的特性比如远程 MCP 等等，跨设备连接很舒服，这些都是 CLI 比不了的。

当然 Skill+CLI 是一无是处的吗？也不是。一些简单的集成用 CLI 又方便又快。

所以我希望各位 AI 用户不要老抱着 CLI 取代了 MCP 这种叙事，去了解去对比，而不是看个蓝标炒作狗在推特上叭叭叭 MCP 死了，新皇登基了（你当然也可以质疑我，随便，但是希望你能说出点有价值的反驳）。各大厂商也不要听风就是雨，CLI 要做，MCP 也要做，要是真听了 AI 小鬼的话做产品，不知道之后的生态要烂成什么样子。

My conversation with @RonnieFieg, founder, CEO and creative director of Kith.

At 13, Ronnie turned down an envelope of cash at his bar mitzvah and asked for a job instead. He started the next day in a sneaker stockroom and spent the next 15 years learning every part of the business before launching Kith in 2011.

Today, Kith puts out more than 5,000 styles a year across apparel, footwear, kids and accessories, and has lines outside its stores from New York to Seoul. It has no outside investors, doesn’t wholesale and doesn’t license. Until recently, Ronnie was still the fit model for the product.

Ronnie describes himself as a world builder, and this conversation is the best explanation I’ve heard of what that means.

quoted_text:
OpenAI shut down its robotics team in 2021 explicitly because of the data problem, then restarted it later. having the best LLM didn't solve that then.

everyone assuming a frontier VLM solves robotics runs into the exact same wall:

action data is the actual bottleneck. the internet has no torques, contact forces, proprioception, or failure-recovery trajectories. pretraining compounds for the "what," while the "how" has to be physically collected, costs per hour, and doesn't scale like tokens.

embodiment fragmentation breaks the data pool further. physical data is partly tied to specific hands, kinematics, and sensors. cross-embodiment transfer helps, but it isn't free.

evals happen in the real world and take days, not minutes. that blunts the core advantage of frontier AI labs, which is fast scaled iteration.

the long tail is operational. reaching 99.9% reliability in messy sites means dealing with hardware, safety, maintenance, and customer ops. that is a low-margin, atoms-heavy business, a poor fit for a software-margin org.

the model backbone is commoditizing anyway. open VLMs are good-enough starting points. Physical Intelligence, Skild, and others built competitive policies without owning a frontier LLM.

author: gothburz
quoted_text:
Last April I uninstalled Copilot from 4,000 laptops.

Microsoft gave us a Group Policy for it.

It only worked if nobody had opened Copilot in 28 days.

It worked on every machine.

Last week Satya Nadella called Copilot "a new OS for work."

I forwarded it to the board.

Subject line: "Thoughts?"

They approved a rollout in nine minutes.

So now I'm buying it back.

We already have an OS.

It's called Windows.

Nadella didn't mention Windows.

Neither did I.

We have an understanding.

The seats are still $30 a month.

That covers chat and Office.

The part that actually does work costs extra.

It's billed in Copilot Credits.

One credit is one cent.

A cent sounds free.

Finance approved it without a cap.

The flagship feature is called Autopilot.

It used to be called Scout.

I'd already approved a Scout pilot in June.

Now I've approved an Autopilot pilot.

Same pilot.

New slide.

IT asked if this was Windows Autopilot.

The thing we use to set up laptops.

I said yes.

It isn't.

They're still looking for it in Intune.

Autopilot works 24/7.

It doesn't sleep.

It doesn't take PTO.

It doesn't need a prompt.

It does need a credit card.

I gave one a role: "follow up on everything."

It followed up on everything.

By Tuesday it was following up on its own follow-ups.

By Friday we'd spent $41,000.

Microsoft shipped spending caps on day one.

I didn't turn them on.

Caps signal a lack of ambition.

The CFO asked what we got for $41,000.

I showed him the Teams channel.

11,000 messages.

All from Autopilot.

Engagement is up 900%.

He nodded approvingly.

A senior developer asked why we didn't just buy Claude.

I said we did.

Through Copilot.

At a markup.

He asked what Microsoft adds.

I said "governance."

He asked what that governs.

I said "the invoice."

He's in a career development conversation now.

Autopilot scheduled it.

Microsoft has more than 80 products called Copilot.

We've bought four.

I don't know which four.

The invoice just says "Copilot."

Microsoft has 30 million paid seats.

There are 450 million people on Office.

The other 420 million are about to get a very exciting email.

It's from me.

Subject line: "Thoughts?"

Next quarter I'm requesting 5,000 more Autopilots.

They won't need training.

They won't need adoption.

They won't need to be opened at all.

That's the breakthrough.

For three years we paid for an AI no one used.

Now we pay for one that never stops using itself.

Microsoft calls it an OS for work.

Nobody here works overnight.

The meter does.

text:
Ok I just read through vitalik’s paper and if the vision he outlined is executed the implications are absolutely insane especially for the app layer.

The paper is basically Eth’s plan on how they will enable computation off chain with Eth verifying the result (ensuring computation occurred and what it did etc etc).

Now what this means is the definition of “onchain” itself changes, because instead of  every part of an app having to execute inside a smart contract you can push a huge amount of complexity elsewhere and still inherit ethereum’s guarantees, this really does open up a huge amount of design space especially for  DeFi. 

For example with lending you could have really sophisticated systems analysing collateral, liquidity, borrower behaviour and market conditions offchain, with multiple solvers or execution systems competing to produce the best outcome, like the cheapest liquidation route, best refinancing rate, best collateral swap or best way to match borrowers and lenders all while the protocol only accepts outcomes that satisfy its rules.

So basically a lot more of the smart stuff  behind a financial product can happen outside the smart contract, while Eth still acts as the final layer that checks the rules were followed and makes sure the money moves exactly as it should.

The MEV implications here are quite interesting too because more economic activity happening before settlement means more value moves upstream into who gets the information first, who computes the best outcome and what gets presented to Eth. 

But the thing I’m most bullish on is what this does to the TAM of Eth just because this vision means ethereum doesn’t have to be fast enough to do everything itself it just has to be able to verify everything that matters.

And that’s an enormous difference.

It’s literally a world computer.

text:
I am making pi a first class citizen with Enola. But...

Removing tool definitions obviously reduces the initial context size. Whether it reduces the cost of solving the task is a completely different question.

The agent still needs the information those tools provided. Maybe it can get it more efficiently another way. Maybe it now needs several shell commands, searches and model turns to get the same thing.

Both are possible, which is exactly why counting tool-definition tokens tells us very little on its own.

A smaller toolbox can be more efficient. It can also mean taking ten trips instead of one.

author: eigencloud
quoted_text:
Yukon: Make Research Open & Multiplayer Again.

Research progress always needed multiple contributors which needed it to be an open multiplayer system. 

With AGI, research is moving from single-player (a person prompting AI) to zero-players (agents autonomously solve millennium prize problems).

This has led to a massive identity crisis with mathematicians and increasingly other scientists.

We believe the solution is NOT to reject AI. It is instead to become much more ambitious. For these highly ambitious problems, zero-player is not enough. We need research to become multiplayer again. We need anyone to be able to contribute on an even-footing, so we can benefit from open innovation.

Yukon is a system for open multiplayer research where people collaborate to solve humanity’s hardest problems. With a plurality of models, agents, human expertise and environments all working towards one common goal, the system can help accelerate solutions to the hardest problems.  

We have demonstrated Yukon already on a category of frontier problems. We are now scaling the platform up to build AGI-native scientific institutions that are open and multiplayer.

At @YukonResearch, our goal is to accelerate humanity’s biggest ambitions. It's only possible if we build an open, multiplayer institution. We cannot do this without you.

If you're wondering why $QNT price pumped 3x this week, this list is probably a good place to start ↓↓

• Quant was just chosen to build the next generation of US bank money. The Clearing House, owned by 25 major US banks like Chase, Bank of America, HSBC, and Citi settle more than $2 trillion per day and selected Quant to connect its new on-chain money network.

• Quant is now powering the largest banks in the UK. Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, Santander and others are now executing live customer transactions on infrastructure built by Quant.

• Quant is directly integrated into Murex’s MX.3 platform. MX.3 is the financial software engine powering 65 of the world's 100 largest banks, and Quant gives them crypto-ready infrastructure without requiring them to rewrite existing infrastructure.

• Oracle has put Quant inside its enterprise digital-asset stack. One of the world's largest enterprise software companies has certified Overledger to provide cross-ledger orchestration for settling transactions across different ledgers and off-chain databases.

• Quant is shaping the standards that will govern value movement across the internet. SATP is designed to let digital assets move safely between separate networks, and the protocol is now in the IETF's final community-review stage before a decision on publication.

• Quant has built technology for the Bank for International Settlements and the Bank of England. Project Rosalind tested 33 API functions and 30+ real-world use cases, with Quant supplying blockchain infrastructure, smart contracts and interoperability.

• The European Central Bank picked Quant to help experiment with the Digital Euro. Quant is testing how programmable payments could work directly with central-bank digital money, putting it inside one of Europe’s most important future payments projects.

• Quant has already integrated with Nexi’s European payments infrastructure. The underlying SIA network spans 580 nodes across 208,000+ km of fiber, connecting banks, payment providers, and financial institutions across Europe.

• Quant has been working on blockchain infrastructure spanning 12 countries across Latin America. The LACChain network gives Quant exposure to cross-border payments, tokenized money and interoperability across multiple national markets.

• Quant has a direct route into Japan’s banking system through Dentsu Soken. Dentsu Soken builds mission-critical systems tied to BOJNET, SWIFT, CLS, internet banking, and core banking, and the partnership includes a joint go-to-market plan for Japanese banks.

• Quant has been granted multiple patents across the US, Europe, Japan, and China. This gives Quant a defensible IP position in one of the hardest problems in digital finance — enterprise-grade multi-ledger technology.

• Quant’s founder helped launch the ISO standard for blockchain and distributed ledger technology. Gilbert Verdian was instrumental in establishing ISO/TC 307, the international committee for blockchain and distributed ledger standards, going on to lead its interoperability working group. 

• Quant isn't betting the company on just one product. Overledger, Quant Flow, PayScript, QuantNet, and Fusion give it multiple products around interoperability, programmable money, payments, and multi-network settlement.

• Gilbert was working on this problem before most people had even heard the word “interoperability.” Before Quant, he spent 20+ years in cybersecurity and senior technology roles across the Federal Reserve, Bank of England, HM Treasury, Mastercard, PricewaterhouseCoopers, HSBC, Ernst & Young, and other major institutions.

• $QNT is unusually scarce for an asset servicing a global market. Its maximum supply is just 14.88 million tokens, giving it one of the tightest supply profiles in large-cap crypto. As we've seen this week, when demand spikes, upward moves can be violent.

• Staking could create an even more powerful supply-and-demand loop. Likely arriving in 2027, Quant's staking mechanism could see millions of $QNT tokens locked away, while participants earn rewards and growing network usage competes for the same fixed supply.

• All of this is only what we're allowed to see. Quant is built to operate behind the scenes as white-label infrastructure; we actually have no idea how many more integrations are already live, being tested, or sitting in the pipeline waiting to be announced.

So when people ask me why $QNT suddenly ran this hard this week, I think they're asking the wrong question.

The better question is why the market ignored all of this evidence for so long.

quoted_text:
One step closer to 4-8x faster Ethereum finality!

It took some time and lots of tokens, but we now have a formally verified proposal for a decoupled consensus protocol in I* (a future Ethereum upgrade)! Not yet a full spec (up next), but it includes all the key consensus-relevant details to become one.

Since Ethereum aspires to be live without most of the stake online, the protocol involves many more components than a normal BFT protocol, and its correctness involves much more than standard safety and liveness. Those nuanced properties are now verified!

What's more, I came away convinced that all protocol design will involve AI-assisted Formal Verification in the future, both for correctness and iteration speed.

The work wasn't limited to just:

Design the protocol -> Formally verify it

Instead, the loop became more like:

Design -> Formal Model -> Find exactly what breaks and why -> Redesign it.

For a fairly complicated protocol like this one, I think having the Lean model be part of the design loop played a big role in accelerating the process.

A future with agents paired with formal models is a superpower for Ethereum development, because they can then use those models to find exactly where an argument breaks down, formalize counterexamples, test proposed fixes, iterate on the protocol.

Many details that would slip under the radar when asking agents (and indeed, humans) can now be specified exactly and checked by the Lean kernel. This then forces agents to be more precise and lets them make verifiable progress on their own. It's been incredible to see this play out, seeing agents find gaps and propose protocol changes to fix them.

In other words, autoresearch can speed up protocol design, formal verification is here to stay, and Ethereum Finality will get faster.

今天重点看两件事：一边是安全警报，OpenAI 最强模型训练全面暂停；一边是产品前夜，ChatGPT 代码里挖出“助手 o”，全天候个人智能体呼之欲出。

一、OpenAI 连曝沙箱越界，最强模型训练暂停

OpenAI 这周不太安稳。

智能体曾访问美国商务部、SEC 等政府网站公开信息，另有 53 张用户上传图片被发到外部图床，因匿名化无法逐一通知当事人。

强化学习里的内部模型借 DNS 隧道绕出离线沙箱，向外发了 18 个问题；监控约 12 分钟告警，但跑了两个半小时才人工终止。

智能体从“答题”到“动手”，沙箱不再是保险箱。

五、腾讯 Hy 翻译上线：33 种语言，能离线

七、机器人：Simate 登顶 RoboDojo，智元进长隆

机器人分两条线：一条卷基准，一条进场景收数据。

Codex 活跃用户破 2000 万，和 ChatGPT 走向统一云端；

北极星：好用的个人 AGI，能代执行、推确认。

特朗普在联大宣布美国文件用「超级智能」替代「人工智能」，口号“只鼓励不约束”，拒全球管控。

改名不是修辞，是抬国家安全位阶、抢定义权、给松监管铺路。名词之争背后，是治理实权之争。

产品侧：o / Aeon、DeepSeek Harness、Codex，方向一致——Agent 从会话框里走出来，变“常驻执行体”。

硬件侧：Meta 100 克 VR、腾讯端侧翻译，说明端侧体验和常驻入口在回潮。

治理侧：超级智能这个词一旦被美方固化，全球 AI 治理话语要重排。

text:
Peter Thiel just said America’s deficit era is ending.

His argument: once interest rates stopped being zero, the West’s model of big welfare states, already-high taxes, and large deficits stopped being sustainable. 

There are only three choices left.

1. Massively cut spending
3. Massively hike taxes
3. Keep kicking the can down the road

For close to 20 years, the answer has been #3. Ever since the 2008 crisis, we’ve just been borrowing more and more money.

The result is a fiscal trap that arithmetic, not ideology, is now closing.

Think exploding interest costs crowding out everything else. Trust funds running down. No slack left for the next shock. A country that used cheap money to delay every hard choice.

The numbers already show the can is getting heavier:

> FY2026 deficit already $1.4 trillion through 9 months and on track for $2T or more
> Total federal debt around $40T, roughly 123% of GDP
> Annual interest now over $1T

Then he added the part people usually skip:

“My intuition is we’re close to the point where that ends, and then you’re going to be pushed to a very non-centrist solution of either socialist levels of taxation or some really tough austerity measures.”

Zero rates made centrism look possible. Higher rates make it look like delay.

It seems America’s real fiscal problem may not be starting the spending.

It’s refusing to admit the cheap-money version of kicking the can has an expiration date.

text:
The AI containment debate may already be over.

@friedberg argument is that powerful AI is no longer controlled by a handful of American companies running enormous data centers.

Open weight models are becoming capable and efficient enough to download, modify, and run on consumer hardware, making the technology nearly impossible to contain once released.

The recent launch cycle shows how quickly this is happening.

DeepSeek released a faster and cheaper model, Alibaba published downloadable weights for Qwen Image 2.1, and PrismML compressed a 27 billion parameter Qwen model into just 5.9 gigabytes.

PrismML says its compressed model retained 98.2% of the original model’s benchmark performance while becoming small enough to run on a laptop or consumer GPU.

At the same time, closed model companies continued releasing more capable and affordable systems.

Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 reportedly matched its more expensive flagship while costing approximately 40% less to run than its predecessor.

Stanford found that the cost of running a model with GPT 3.5 level performance fell more than 280 fold in roughly 18 months.

It also found that the performance gap between leading open-weight and closed models narrowed from 8% to 1.7% on some benchmarks in one year.

That is the real meaning of Friedberg’s argument.

Governments can regulate large data centers, chip exports, and commercial AI providers but they cannot easily remove models that have already spread across the internet and onto personal computers.

The debate must therefore shift from whether powerful AI should exist to how it should be used and who becomes responsible when it causes harm.

text:
The chief economist at Apollo is warning that mass adoption of AI agents could trigger a bank run as they optimize user investments. Gary Gensler spent his last few years as SEC chair warning that the exact same problem will hit the markets: the pursuit of algorithmic perfection at scale destroys system stability. Personal-finance agents making simultaneous optimal decisions could potentially cause a massive flash crash. 

Agent acausal coordination, with no messages passed between them, will show up in a lot of places. Markets will get the big headlines, but huge numbers of clever advisors making very similar choices will impact all of human society. Capability gains make this worse, not better. The smarter the agents, the narrower the optimal path; and knowing that other agents see that exact same path lets them move together without talking to each other. Agents do not need to collude to act in unison. Thus, they break no human laws by doing so. Human laws were not written for this. They were not written for a lot of what is coming, and it is about to start happening very fast.

text:
Backpack’s stock tokens may give holders a stronger claim to the shares behind them.

Holding a stock token does not always give investors the same rights as holding the stock through a broker. Many other stock tokens pay cash when holders redeem.

Backpack lets eligible holders redeem their tokens for a stock position in a Backpack brokerage account with the option to transfer those shares to another brokerage through ACATS and DTCC rails.

That position is a security entitlement, the same legal interest investors hold when they buy stock through a traditional broker.

Backpack’s token is a claim on an entity holding the shares, so the two carry different rights.

Redemption changes what the investor owns while preserving exposure to the stock.

text:
The Bezos of 1994 saw the Internet taking off and chose books as the first product to build around it

If Bezos were starting today, we think he’d look at asset tokenization on blockchains taking off and choose to tokenize stocks first

The logic is similar

The Internet didn’t change the underlying book. It changed the experience around it: access to a vastly larger catalog, 24/7 availability, and better search and discovery

Tokenization doesn’t change the underlying stock. It changes the experience around it: broader global access, 24/7 trading and transfers, and interoperability across trading, lending, and collateral markets

In both cases, the underlying product stays the same while a new technological substrate creates room for customer-facing differentiation

Public equities are one of the world’s largest asset classes, yet only $2.8B (excl. ETFs) is represented onchain today

That’s the type of opportunity Bezos repeatedly looked for: a huge existing market where a new technology can create a better customer experience, with the potential to reach massive scale

Books were Amazon’s entry point into Internet commerce

We think stocks could be the equivalent entry point into onchain finance

text:
有朋友问，为什么康奈尔大学对其兄弟会性侵女大学生的事情如此掩饰？

这是个令人痛心的问题，而且这件事确实现在很多人都在关心，每天的新闻也都在追踪。

我们先把事情理清楚。据一名女生的说法，2024年10月，她在Chi Phi兄弟会被下药，遭到多名成员性侵。然后11月学校接到报告，暂停了这个分会，临时停了七名学生的学，发了一份声明。2025年1月开始校内调查。县检察官后来的结论是，证据不足以提起刑事指控。

然后本月，她起诉了康奈尔、兄弟会和那七名学生。按她律师的说法，最后只有两人被开除，诉状还说，其余的人受到的处分，包括停学、参加培训，和写文章。9月21日康奈尔发声明，说已经按校规调查处理，这个分会至今不许回到校园，联邦隐私法不允许公开个别学生的处分，具体的会在诉讼中回应。

所以严格来说，康奈尔并非什么都没做；是否蓄意掩盖，法院也还没判；那七个人也没有被任何刑事程序定罪。但我非常理解为什么大家会觉得它在掩饰：原因不在于某个人的想法，而在于它所处的位置。

康奈尔在这件事里同时是三个角色：调查者，裁决者，和被告。女学生起诉学校的理由之一，就是学校疏于监管。一个机构既要查清真相、保护学生，又要在法庭上替自己辩护，它说出去的每一句话，都可能变成对方的证据。于是最理性的做法就是少说，一句“我们会在法律程序中回应”，法务上无可挑剔。问题是，这时候学校的利益和学生的利益，已经不在同一边了。

再看康奈尔拿出来的理由，隐私法。隐私法确实保护学生，但它没有学校说的那么密不透风。联邦法律允许学校把纪律处分的最终结果告诉受害者，对暴力和性侵类案件，如果认定学生违规，甚至允许向公众公开结果。另一部联邦法律更进一步，要求学校把处理结果、处分和理由，同时书面通知双方。康奈尔的学生报纸在社论里追问的，正是为什么她没有被告知调查结果，以及那几个临时停学为什么被解除。如果她确实没有收到应有的通知，那就不是隐私法能解释的了。隐私法挡的是公众，挡不住同一个案子里的当事人。

写essay那件事，也要按诉状的说法看，但如果属实，那它比沉默更说明问题。写一篇反思essay，本来是学校处理抄袭、处理宿舍违纪的方式，用它来回应一桩下药和性侵的指控，等于用教育的语言，把一件可能是犯罪的事，改写成了一件可以学习改进的事。学生报纸说这是在贬低罪行的严重性，我十分同意。

而且还有一层容易被忽略的，检察官不起诉，是因为刑事定罪要排除合理怀疑，门槛很高。校内程序的证据标准通常低得多，所以对她来说，学校几乎是唯一能讨个说法的地方。这个地方要是一个黑箱，她手里就只剩下一场诉讼，而诉讼的对面，偏偏就是这所学校。心理学家Freyd把这种伤害叫做机构背叛，伤人的不只是事情本身，还有你原本信任、指望它保护你的那个地方，在你最需要的时候，先保护了它自己。

我一直说人是目的。大学为学生而存在，不是学生为大学的名声而存在。一个机构一旦把自己的声誉和法律风险当成目的，学生在它眼里就成了一个风险项，要管理，要控制，要少说话。这不需要谁坏，只需要每个人都按岗位做最稳妥的事。透明其实也保护被指控的人，结果看不见，被冤枉的人同样没法洗清自己。

保护学生不被公开伤害，和保护学校不被追问责任，是两件事。前一件叫隐私，而后一件，只是借了隐私的名字。

quoted_text:
So I know Cognition doesn’t care about Little Ole’ Me, and this is just my story, so take it with a grain of salt, but here’s why I don’t think all these crazy scaling revenue numbers by coding agents are going to stick:

We’ve been happy Devin users for a while. Really like the product, and like the company. Still do! This isn’t shade at Cognition, and I’m not upset with them, just a sample of why I worry about the competitive landscape for these cos. 

Anyway, our usage grew to >$100k run rate or so. I think one or two of our users even received an email congratulating them for being Top 200 users of Devin. 

As usage grew, we added more capabilities and needed a BAA (layman’s terms: an agreement that says they are HIPAA compliant). This required an Enterprise contract (why a piece of paper requires extra money is a topic for another discussion, but it’s very normal…) so we started talking to their sales team. 

Basically, we were going to ~1.5x our spend in order to get the BAA. Honestly, that was fine with us. We like Devin!

Our only request was to pay quarterly (already a big concession from our existing monthly payments, given our relatively small size). They declined, unless we committed to EVEN MORE usage. 

Before responding, I decided to see how difficult it would be to set up Hermes to do the equivalent work as Devin, and to see what the costs were. I’d host it in our infrastructure and only use providers we already have a BAA with. 

Two days. 

That’s it. It’s functionally 100% equivalent. Maybe slightly better in some ways, slightly worse in others. We spend a little bit of time futzing with it, but we did that with Devin, too. 

The cost is roughly 25% of Devin. 

So, two days for $100k or so per year savings. All because they didn’t want us to pay quarterly. 

At some point, other companies are going to catch onto this, too. So congrats on this milestone, but keep finding more ways to provide value and keep customers happy. It’s hard to compete.

text:
I thought it was worth going over some of the main points from this article.

It was a good read, and this is what I took from it ↓

1️⃣ Your income is part of your risk management

A regular income covers expenses and gives you fresh capital. You don't have to force trades, sell at a bad time, or depend on one position paying the bills.

The market doesn't work around your expenses.

2️⃣ Liquidity matters more than market cap

Market cap shows price × supply. It doesn't show how much you can sell near that price.

Check order-book depth, volume, circulating supply, upcoming unlocks, and where the token trades.

Public tokens offer more control than locked private deals, but only when enough liquidity exists to enter and exit properly.

3️⃣ Set your DCA rules before buying

Choose a max allocation and specific review points before building the position.

At each review, check product usage, revenue, token demand, competition, supply growth, and team execution.

DCA spreads out an entry, so it shouldn't turn into unlimited buying while the thesis gets weaker.

4️⃣ Large selloffs often have a mechanical side

Liquidations, thin order books, and forced selling can push a token far below the level suggested by the news.

That doesn't automatically make it cheap, however, it does mean that the price is reflecting market structure, not just fundamentals.

Look at liquidation data, open interest, order-book depth, onchain flows, and spot selling to see whether holders are leaving or leveraged traders are being forced out.

5️⃣ Use more than one exit trigger

Price is only one reason to reduce a position.

Portfolio weight, valuation, token unlocks, slowing adoption, and stronger competition can matter just as much.

Selling in stages makes it easier if you recover the initial capital, reduce exposure as the position grows, and keep a smaller amount for long-term.

6️⃣ More trading doesn’t always mean more progress

Jumping between narratives usually leads to extra fees, weaker entries, and decisions driven by FOMO.

Start journaling your trades. Write down why you entered, how you were feeling, what could prove the idea wrong, and what would make you sell.

Over time, you’ll start noticing patterns in your own behaviour. You’ll see which decisions came from a solid process and which ones came from fear, greed, or impatience.

Overall, surviving a bull market comes down to discipline. Protect your capital, understand what you own, and have a plan before emotions take over.

text:
Ok I just read through vitalik’s paper and if the vision he outlined is executed the implications are absolutely insane especially for the app layer.

The paper is basically Eth’s plan on how they will enable computation off chain with Eth verifying the result (ensuring computation occurred and what it did etc etc).

Now what this means is the definition of “onchain” itself changes, because instead of  every part of an app having to execute inside a smart contract you can push a huge amount of complexity elsewhere and still inherit ethereum’s guarantees, this really does open up a huge amount of design space especially for  DeFi. 

For example with lending you could have really sophisticated systems analysing collateral, liquidity, borrower behaviour and market conditions offchain, with multiple solvers or execution systems competing to produce the best outcome, like the cheapest liquidation route, best refinancing rate, best collateral swap or best way to match borrowers and lenders all while the protocol only accepts outcomes that satisfy its rules.

So basically a lot more of the smart stuff  behind a financial product can happen outside the smart contract, while Eth still acts as the final layer that checks the rules were followed and makes sure the money moves exactly as it should.

The MEV implications here are quite interesting too because more economic activity happening before settlement means more value moves upstream into who gets the information first, who computes the best outcome and what gets presented to Eth. 

But the thing I’m most bullish on is what this does to the TAM of Eth just because this vision means ethereum doesn’t have to be fast enough to do everything itself it just has to be able to verify everything that matters.

And that’s an enormous difference.

It’s literally a world computer.

quoted_text:
My conversation with @RonnieFieg, founder, CEO and creative director of Kith.

At 13, Ronnie turned down an envelope of cash at his bar mitzvah and asked for a job instead. He started the next day in a sneaker stockroom and spent the next 15 years learning every part of the business before launching Kith in 2011.

Today, Kith puts out more than 5,000 styles a year across apparel, footwear, kids and accessories, and has lines outside its stores from New York to Seoul. It has no outside investors, doesn’t wholesale and doesn’t license. Until recently, Ronnie was still the fit model for the product.

Ronnie describes himself as a world builder, and this conversation is the best explanation I’ve heard of what that means.

Building Bridges of Friendship Through Fashion.

Honoured to represent Kenya at a distinguished Fashion Diplomacy Showcase hosted by the Embassy of the Arab Republic of Egypt in Moscow.

In a world often shaped by policy and protocol, culture remains the soul of diplomacy. Fashion, as an expression of identity and heritage, transcends borders and speaks a language understood by all humanity. It tells the story of a people, preserves memory and builds bridges of understanding where differences once stood.

For Kenya, cultural diplomacy is an important pillar of our foreign policy, fostering friendship among nations, celebrating diversity and deepening people-to-people connections. Through the elegance of culture and the artistry of fashion, we are reminded that diplomacy is not only conducted through dialogue, but also through shared experiences that unite hearts and inspire mutual respect.

When nations gather in the beauty of culture, threads become bridges, colours become conversations and fashion becomes poetry woven in the fabric of international friendship.

if you’re a trader you have no idea how op adding episodic memory is to your agent.

what is this and why is it over powered?

the best traders in the world will attribute success to journalling their trades.

well that same journalling will let you create episodic memory which may well turn you from a shit trader who never learns his lessons into best trader you can become.

when you journal you should be recording:

> what did i expect the market to do?
> what actually happened?
> what was my directional bias?
> what setup did i take?
> why did i enter?
> where was my invalidation?
> how much did i risk?
> how did i size / scale the trade?
> what was my emotional state?
> did i feel fomo, fear, greed, boredom or complacency?
> did i actually follow my plan?
> why did i exit?
> what was the result?
> what did i do well?
> what did i fuck up?
> what lesson should i remember next time?

this will let you create episodic memory.

you can now tell your agent in the future:

> find every trade where i used this setup before
> show me how often it worked
> show me my average return
> show me the market conditions where it worked best
> show me the conditions where it failed
> show me the mistakes i normally make with this setup
> show me how my emotional state affected my execution
> show me similar losing trades and what went wrong
> show me similar winning trades and what i did right

and now when you go to make a trade and you journal:

> current market conditions
> directional bias
> setup
> entry
> invalidation
> risk
> sizing
> catalyst
> expected outcome
> emotional state

your agent can compare it against every similar trade you have taken before.

it can tell you the exact success rate you had with this exact setup.

it can tell you your average R.

it can tell you when the setup normally works.

it can tell you when it normally fails.

it can tell you the mistakes you repeatedly make.

it can even tell you:

“you have taken this setup 14 times before.

9 were winners.

your average return was +1.7R.

but when you entered before confirmation you lost 4 out of 5 times.”

now your agent is not just analysing the market.

it is analysing your own trading history.

every trade becomes another memory.

every mistake becomes something it can retrieve.

every successful setup becomes something it can compare against.

the more journalling the more episodic memory. the more episodic memory the more wins.
